And tell me now all those things: the shipwright, how he sets the timbers in order; the builder, how he sets the stones in order; the chorus-trainer; whomever you please. For whatever of these you mention, you will be speaking on behalf of Cimon's leadership and public conduct. And indeed, when you say that this whole is called Cosmos, "order," you say rightly, as I for my part affirm, leading us on toward doing nothing at random; Cimon, then, preserved for the city what corresponds to the name of the universe. For he made all as orderly as he could. Such was his public conduct, and such things he taught both the people in the city and his followers on the campaigns. "But, by Zeus, they ostracized him, that for ten years they might not hear his voice." And again they brought him back before the ten years were out, that they might hear his voice — so much did they long for it. But you speak of how they condemned him, while you do not consider how they changed their minds. And the things they unjustly voted against both men you mention, but the things they rightly resolved you do not think are, for those who were driven out, an excuse, and for the one acquitted the greatest proof of virtue. And, it seems, those who —

condemned themselves repented and did not abide by what they had resolved at first; but you have brought your charge as though it were something authoritative, and you did not think fit in this to imitate the Athenians by acquitting the man of the charge, but what was harsher you imitated of them, and the rest you let go — and this, what is most absurd of all, while accusing the very Athenians, and, what is finer, not these second things but those which one would gladly attribute to Cimon. And if nothing of this kind had happened, you would have had nothing to accuse; but since they dissolved the event by their repentance and transferred the blame to themselves, do you not reckon it equal as if we had had nothing to say from the first? And surely it is far greater and finer, for the account of virtue, to have fallen and returned than not to have fled at all. For the latter belongs even to ordinary men, surely, while this was not according to the many; and the one a man might reckon to fortune, but this to being recognized as superior to the rest. For of the falling and fleeing, envy is the cause, and perhaps some other such thing might appear; but of the recall and summons before the time, there is nothing else to allege but virtue, on account of which they were ashamed in his absence and supposed his presence profitable to themselves, and, the greatest thing, thought fit to condemn themselves rather than him. So that if one must consider him by himself, what need is there to speak, if anyone offended against him? But if one must contemplate him from the rest, this man appears honored above all others. But not yet these things; for presently they will perhaps fit better. But what, of the many and great things for which one might justly praise Cimon, is the greatest and, as it were, the chief head, and belongs preeminently to that man, this I wish still to say and to render to the man as something else his due. For in few of all men, as it seems to me, both of the earlier and of the later, does this argument hold and not contend along with it nor give room to the slander, that —

it is, as it were, fated for the sons of noble and good men to turn out base and worth little of their fathers' virtue — he who, being the son of Miltiades and inheriting so great a peril of that man's glory, disgraced nothing of what he had, nor thought it enough to inscribe his father's name, like one claiming to win at Olympia because he is the son of an Olympic victor; but he so well and so beautifully imitated that man, and clung as it were to the tracks of his father's deeds, that even if none of the historians had happened to say whose son he was, one could from the deeds themselves conjecture his father and to whom he belonged. But our argument has come round to Miltiades himself, whom I should be more ashamed to praise than to blame; so much do I think I should say less than I wish in every way. And yet so much I would say confidently: for if Plato, rising up — I say — shall himself think fit to accuse Miltiades and shall judge this to be the better argument for him, I am ready to concede everything and not to think that man worth very much. But it does not seem to me that he would easily do so, who, even when he mentioned him, said: "Miltiades, the one at Marathon." And yet this is nearer to a kind of lament than to a reproach, and to one honoring rather than disparaging, like those whom Simonides was wont to honor in his epigrams. Nevertheless Miltiades too has a share in the catalogue, and there has come round to him the lot of the —

Plataeans who were marshaled by him at that time. For, no accusation against him having been spoken beforehand, he is in a way of necessity put on trial, because his name is among the servants. And yet, Plato, one of the forensic men might say, he who laid down the law did rightly in thinking fit that the suits and the indictments should be expressed plainly: "So-and-so injured me by doing this and that"; "and he proposed these illegal measures"; and if anyone brings any other charge, to state it in the same manner and not to frighten men idly. But you put off declaring, it seems, until the morrow what each of these men did or said to do wrong — as in some other dialogue — and you accuse them all in common, and not even him whom you thought fit to honor above the others, Pericles, by apportioning the charges to him and laying more of them on him than on any, not even him did you convict, nor did you show by saying or doing what he made them such; but by this one thing you honored him beyond the rest, making the charges against him more numerous and, as it were, clearer, so that one knows about what one must speak. But he has perhaps had no less even from us, so that in this respect one could not greatly blame the one who furnished the starting-point. So be it. But Miltiades, the one at Marathon — where in the chorus shall we station him, or in what rank? Or is it clear that the one before the theater and where it will be in a fine position for viewing for all? — except in so far that the man is not one to stand on the left rather than on the right wing for the Greeks. And, by Zeus, if anyone should question him and lead him back step by step from the beginning, as Plato is wont to question — by teaching what, or counseling what, —

did he make the Athenians better, or by leading and rearing them straightway from youth, or what sorts of customs and pursuits did he introduce into the city — we should say that he would not be at a loss for a measured and true answer, but would answer thus; and we shall write down for Miltiades the answers in the verses: "I shall, then, tell of the ancient education, how it was disposed, / when I flourished speaking what is just, and self-control was the custom. / First it was required that no one should hear the voice of a boy uttering a sound; / next, that they should walk in the streets in good order to the music-master's, / the lads of the same quarter, naked, in a body, even if it snowed like meal." Then concerning the music of that time, of what sort it was — that not the all-harmonious nor what aimed at pleasure was honored in it, but one had to sing either "Pallas, sacker of cities, terrible," or "some far-resounding shout," straining the harmony which the fathers handed down. "And if any of them played the buffoon or bent some bending, / he was thrashed with many blows, as one doing away with the Muses." Sitting at the trainer's, and so on, going through each of the rest, he will at the end set upon some of those who are vexed: "But yet these are those things / from which my training reared the men who fought at Marathon." Such things Miltiades will answer — to me neither otherwise base nor anywhere false, but befitting both him to have given this training, being a leader in those times, and the Athenians, long since educated, to come to the battle. For it was not possible, not possible, for men to become orderly and brave and superior to terrors in a single day, having been reared from the first in indolence and basely in —

all respects, but it was necessary that they should long beforehand have been laid hold of both by good nurture and by fitting words and by measured habits and by the best opinions. At any rate none of the Dolopians met them on that day, nor any of the others reared like them. Nor indeed was Datis, the master and leader of the enemy's camp, able either himself to become a brave man in a single day or to make those under him such, many as they were. And yet it had been told him beforehand by the King that he would be deprived of his head if he did not bring back the Eretrians and Athenians. But nonetheless fear made him no better. For those were temporary injunctions from a master, but Miltiades had long since persuaded the Athenians to consider no master but the laws, and to think no fear stronger than the beautiful and the just, nor any necessity so strong on account of which it would be fitting to become worse. For these reasons he had the means to use them. For he could not so suddenly have made them sailors, not even if it had been very necessary that they be sailors on that day, nor musicians, nor horsemen. Nor, then, good hoplites, nor, to sum up, good men profitable to themselves, could so brief a time have sufficed to make; but just as the farmers reap the fruit of their seeds many months later and not at the moment of casting them down, so too Miltiades, having laid hold of those men by old agreements, had them useful at the crisis, not taking up their lessons at the moment of need — for the chorus would have contended shamefully for him in that case — but having trained them at leisure for the need. And indeed of their training and care all Greece reaped the common fruits. And surely, even if one had nothing else to say of Miltiades, nor were it possible to find many and dignified things, it seems to me enough that the decree should stand, instead of an image —

of his soul, for all. Or, in the gods' name, shall we think fit that the spirit and strength of our speeches and writings be esteemed, and if there is anything in them tending toward courage or justice, shall we say it is not useless to those who wish to use it — but of that man's purpose and intention, of what sort it was and whether to be imitated by ordinary men or by the more virtuous, is the decree not a sufficient sign, which he composed in the very midst of the dangers, declaring one judgment to the Greeks concerning all that is just? And surely, if it is right to honor ancestors, how is it not right to honor Miltiades as a common ancestor of the Greeks who came after those times? For he who not only presided over their safety, but also showed of what sort men ought to be in the struggles for freedom, and set up a clear example for all, this man is most manifestly of all those of old. If, then, we praise both Solon and Lycurgus for the laws they laid down, how is it not just to praise Miltiades, who in deed laid down this law, that no one should admire the worse nor choose the easiest before the better? For let us examine Miltiades by comparison with Lycurgus. For surely it cannot be said of him either that Plato set him as one of the servants — this is not so, nor near it. Lycurgus, then, because he laid down laws looking toward courage and endurance, and because he made the citizens better in the affairs of war, is thus of good repute — like some trainer who has prepared others for victory, but has himself displayed nothing of the kind. But Miltiades, besides accustoming the citizens to the best things and preparing them to be inferior to none in the affairs of war, was himself the leader of the greatest of deeds —

he plainly was. So he appears to us to have become not by much second to Lycurgus, nor among any others more justly of good repute than among those who justly praise that man. And indeed, in the other works — I mean both pursuits and arts — some were honored as having begun, others as having surpassed; but Homer they praise as having both begun and brought poetry to completion as beautifully as possible. Miltiades, then, both himself began the freedom for the Greeks and left to none of the Greeks any surpassing of his own deeds — not, at least, among those we can name from the other cities. So that I fear it may be of a piece, neither to receive Homer into the city nor to be willing to praise Miltiades. Then Plato asks whom Miltiades made better, whether of the citizens or of the strangers, or whether he means slave or free, or man or woman. Whom, then, Plato, did Miltiades make worse, whether of the citizens or of the strangers — whether I mean slave or free, or man or woman? Or did association with him end in reproach and loss to any of them all? And I shall answer you brilliantly: whom did Miltiades make better? And I would not name man and woman to you, like those who inquire about small works, but, if you grant me to say it, that man made all the Athenians better and the whole city better, as I speak of a city and as I speak of a people and as it is meant of the commonwealth. For do not make me go through everything with precision, nor by a single measure, nor, like Geryon's heads, equal through...

You should not suppose that all men must stand in a single rank; rather, leave room for some who are inferior, since not all men are alike in war. Just so, neither in a city are all alike in judgment, any more than all bodies are equal and nearly the same; but as among the leaders themselves some are worse and some are better, so a people too could never become precisely one, but of necessity some are worse and some are better disposed in the very matter of obeying their leaders. Suppose, then, that under the leadership of Miltiades as well some drew the greatest profit from his power, others a moderate amount, and within the middle range too set down a further variation. And in a multitude one man might be less fortunate even in respect of his hearing. The sun itself cannot warm all men alike; before now a man has shivered in the clear light of noon when a chill came over him. If you examine the matter in this measured way, with regard to the power of nature, Miltiades too will appear to you to have benefited the whole city. But if you look for the best men one by one, you will not find even the Thessalian horses all excellent in a row, nor the Laconian hounds; yet the name is preserved for the breeds all the same. So examine the Athenians too in this way, looking at the whole character of their polity and how they conducted their common affairs in those times—just as we say, indeed, that a city is well governed, although it is not possible for such a city to exist in which no fault, greater or smaller, occurs, and no one does wrong at all. And further, on your own terms, you wise men, one might bring the argument round to this point: that if a city is to be well governed, then all who dwell in it must be law-abiding, both men and women; and if law-abiding, then orderly; and if orderly, then temperate; and if temperate, then prudent as well; and if all are prudent, surely no one can do wrong; so that, as long as the city is well governed, of necessity no one

does any wrong at all. But I do not think this is possible, nor would you ever say that, because it does not come about, therefore no city should be held to be well governed; rather, examining the common form of the polity, and at the same time judging the city against the other cities, you reckon some things, I think, to the laws and customs, and assign others to the necessities of nature. If you consider the Athenians in this way too, and do not cross-examine them man by man as the lawgivers do, I have a further addition to make to you, greater still and more wonderful: that Miltiades made not only the city better, but, besides the city, all Greece as well. And as you ask which of the citizens or of the foreigners he improved, so I declare that both the citizens and all the other Greeks were made better by that man. For he led them all toward the noblest things, so that he made no one worse, but, so far as in him lay, made all better. But look at the matter from your own definitions, paying no heed to my arguments, except where something follows from necessity. Do you say anything throughout your whole discourse other than this: that justice is noble, and that whatever a man does he must do with justice, and must always use rhetoric for the sake of what is just? "Even if a man strikes me," you say, "it makes a difference whether justly or not; and if a man drives me into exile, then, if unjustly, he is wretched"; and everywhere you employ these qualifications, saying "justly" or "unjustly." And the just you rightly hold to be noble, and its opposite base; and justice you make the mark of a happy man, injustice of his opposite; and the one you say a man must pursue as far as he can, the other flee with all the speed he has. Are not these your arguments? Do you not praise all things done justly, and blame them when done otherwise? Hold, then, and consider; for let us not, as in a battle by night, lay hands on our own friends. Is it just, then, to ward off attackers? Most just of all. And what of this—is it not just to make more account of the Greeks than of the barbarians? Anyone, surely, at least anyone who is Greek, would say so. Miltiades, then, when the barbarians were attacking the

Greeks, set nothing before the common safety, nor did he privately deliberate about his own affairs, nor put off to another occasion the showing of his own virtue. And yet it was open to him, had he looked not to the best but pursued the same ends as the tyrants, to join—if he wished—with Hippias and the Peisistratids in marching against Greece; or, if he wished, to come with the Aleuadae out of Thessaly, or before the Aleuadae. Nor, I think, would he have lacked men of the same mind even from Lacedaemon. And indeed the barbarians would have received him no less gladly than many others. But, as it seems, Miltiades did not think these things became him; rather, letting all this go and passing it by and judging it worth nothing in the reckoning of virtue, he gave himself to the common service of his fatherland and of the Greeks. And yet, in doing this and choosing this, did he display a mark of justice and nobility, or of vice and injustice? Or shall we say of neither? For my part, I think nothing prevents him from being called happy and enviable, if the saying of Plato is true—that a bright glory rests upon those who have served their city justly. So be it. But shall we have fears for his courage, or shall we say that the occasions which displayed it were small and trifling? Were not, I may almost say, all men at that time fallen beneath the Persians, and did not the king accomplish most things by his command? Wherever they set out, they supposed they held the place; and even those who marched against the Scythians were thought to have failed only because they could not find them. The Egyptians, the wisest of all men, did not find a single device among them all by which to escape slavery. And of Libya

there was then no account that divided it from Asia; rather, all was one continent, so far as the Persians were concerned. Of the Greeks, those who dwelt in Asia were enslaved—some for three generations, some for longer; the islands were of no consequence; the Eretrians, of the Euboeans, who had raised their hands in resistance, were carried off, household and all, within three days; of the others in Europe, some had already given earth and water, while others were watching for what was to come, accounting themselves more fortunate than the Eretrians only insofar as they would suffer the same things later. The Lacedaemonians, whether on account of the war against the Messenians or because they were waiting for the full moon, were themselves unable to come to the rescue. And the army had already put in at Marathon from Eretria, on equal terms. That was no time for servants, nor for submissive men, nor for those who had long known how to do what they were bidden, nor for those who look to what seems good to others, nor for those who seek how they may live in safety and think this sufficient; rather, that occasion, like a herald, summoned the bravest of the Greeks and him who had longest consorted with the best reasonings, and one who knew how a man must both save and be saved. Nor do we praise those men—I mean those who led in those times—for this, that they saved Greece in any way whatever, like the pilot you speak of who brings a cargo from Aegina or from the Pontus; rather for this, that they saved both the citizens and all men with nobility of bearing. For if they had thought it right to save them by surrendering their arms, or by coming to terms with the heralds, or by choosing the Persian king as master in place of their laws, I for one would not have thought I ought to congratulate either the words that persuaded or those who were persuaded, on their safety; rather, I would have been able to call those men servants in truth, and hirelings of the passing day, like the ferrymen—and not only, if you like, the pilots. But if, beginning with the heralds themselves and with the answer given

they proclaimed to the Athenians that they must practice for the contest on behalf of the freedom of the Greeks, and must not abandon the post of their high spirit, nor throw away their arms nor yield to their fears, but take up their arms and become superior to their fears—or rather, count this one fear alone, terrible and unbearable, namely to yield to baser men and to give up their ancestral bearing—if, saying these things and so prepared, they thought it right to meet the decision concerning all things and to receive whatever should come, as men who would gain alike in either event, then I do not see what ignoble service there is in this, or how it resembles the reckonings of a pilot. But if you mean this—that in the same way as in a ship the pilot is supreme, and to him belong all matters, both those of the sailors and those of the passengers, so too at that time the affairs of the Greeks came into the hands of those men and were directed by their judgment—if you mean this, and use the pilot only as an illustration, just as Homer likens men to lions and boars and many other things, not once for all, but so far as suits his purpose, if in this respect you too remember the pilot, then I grant and concede it. But if you misuse the comparison in all the same respects, and assign the same standard of justice to both, I do not know who will accept this—and I think not even you yourself. "The pilot," you say, "having taken two obols or a few drachmas, is discharged of his duty." But Miltiades did not, for two obols nor for a couple of drachmas—nor, I think, for any great sum of money—conduct his policy among the Athenians, or rather, if the truth must be told, among all the Greeks; rather he offered his virtue unpaid into the common stock for Greece, just as you say Socrates offered himself to the young. "The pilot," you say, "makes no better men of those who embark on the ship." Excellently put, Plato—and yet the pilot too perhaps makes the sailors better in seamanship at least. But I let this pass. Grant that the pilot makes no one any better; yet Miltiades, even before entering upon the danger, trained them all toward what was best, and, having led out men who were, so to speak, private persons,

brought them back victorious. Do not, then, my good sir, set him on a level with the pilot who carries men to Olympia; rather let us say he resembles the trainer who, having long prepared the athlete for the contest there, then led him out and brought him back a victor. And if there is added to this the further fact that he himself perished while winning the first place of the contest at the same Olympiad—Heracles! who could charge such a man with mere servitude, or who would not rejoice with him over his crowns? It is not possible for the pilot to say to any of the passengers that they must despise death, nor that they should throw themselves on purpose into the sea—only to throw out so much of the gear, and this for the safety of their bodies; so far the pilot has authority to command. But the sum of the matter has been laid down for him beforehand by his art: to save, and not to meddle. But in the words of Miltiades there was none of this—to be saved by every means, not even at the cost of throwing away their arms, should it so chance. Far from it. Rather the very opposite: not to seek to be saved by every means, but, even if they must die, to dare it on behalf of fatherland and temples and tombs and polity. You see how far he has surpassed even the pilot. And so all who were persuaded of this by him lie august in their august rest, having ended their life most nobly of all the Greeks, possessing their tomb as a monument of their virtue, and, though beneath the earth, guarding the earth itself, not held captive by it—coming closest to sharing in that address which Hesiod made for the end of the golden race, when he said: "These are called the holy spirits beneath the earth, noble, averters of evil, guardians of mortal men." And if you call those men all but spirits—nay, daemonic—you may say with confidence that they are certain guardians beneath the earth and saviors of the Greeks, averters of evil and

wholly good, and that they protect the land no worse than Oedipus who lies at Colonus, or any other who is believed to lie somewhere in the land for a season for the benefit of the living. And they seem to me so far to have surpassed Solon the founder that, whereas he, sown in Salamis, is thought to guard the island for the Athenians, these men, having fallen for the post to which they were assigned, preserved all Attica—nay, all the rest of Greece besides—not only by what they themselves contributed, nor by their hindering of the invaders, but because they also showed those who came after what kind of men they must be when like occasions arose. And indeed, when even for the dead among them the gain did not fall to the ground, but they themselves enjoyed the benefit of their own purpose, and all the rest the benefit of theirs, how much greater was the advantage that accrued to those at least who lived and conquered! And for my part I think that Heracles and Pan and those who came to the battle and shared the command with Miltiades are sufficient witnesses of his courage before all mankind, and that this brings to Miltiades no less

honor for his whole conduct of the city than the saying that brings honor to Pindar for his music—that this same god danced one of his songs for him. And indeed Plato's own voice says that Pan, son of Hermes, is skilled in speech; and elsewhere he says that he is reason itself, or at least brother to reason. This god, then, plainly so delighted in Miltiades himself—which he would not have done, surely, had he seen him to be a worthless man in respect of speech. Therefore he bears witness to all at once: that the rhetorical art is indeed an art, and not an artless knack; that Miltiades was both a craftsman of speech, and that his courage in deeds was a near match for his words. Is it then better, in the sight of men or of gods, to speak ill of Miltiades? One might think it strange that the Athenians, on the strength of these deeds, founded the temple to Pan, having taken thought no sooner; while Plato, with these deeds of Miltiades before him, dares to say the baser things and is so far from honoring him that, for his own part, he robs him even of the honor that justly belongs to him—him who, though one of ten generals, is named, so to speak, alone, and that too with Aristides son of Lysimachus present, whom not even Plato thought fit to single out for blame among them all, but was ashamed to do so. Yet that man was conspicuous at Plataea as a general beside Pausanias, whereas at Marathon he was hidden beneath Miltiades and did not dispute for an equal share, being just, as you say, and indeed doing what was just in this very thing. For he who pressed for the battle to be fought and did not allow the cause to be ruined by delay, and who took all upon himself and showed that very thing which you sing in your oracles—that a man ought not to place his hopes in others, by whose good or ill fortune both he and what is his must needs go astray, but in himself, the man who is temperate and brave and prudent—Miltiades is that one man, no other

at all. And for this very reason he alone of them all, as they say, was chosen to be painted with his hand stretched out, as he happened then to be exhorting the soldiers. So that man was a good orator not only on the Pnyx, in the assembly, but also at Marathon, and everywhere displayed the excellence of speech intact. And then, the Athenians buried those of their own who fell that day in that very place, and did not mingle them with the others who lie in the public tombs, but, deeming them to be greater in virtue than the rest, judged them worthy of a private honor as well; yet you did not blush to set the leader of these men—the man who began for all the Greeks the most necessary and at the same time the noblest things: safety, freedom, glory—among the cooks, and you think it not enough unless you also cast about him the utmost reproaches of slavery. What are you saying? Miltiades a slave—through whom Greece was not enslaved? And did he pass his life serving the Athenians—he through whom the Athenians did not serve the Persians in the most shameful tasks, and through whom Datis was unable to render to the king the service that had been laid upon him? And shall we enroll in the guild of the cosmeticians a man so grimy and dust-covered, more fittingly than any one of the wrestlers and the men of the gymnasium? We should indeed incur great absurdity. Consider this too—how great a proof it is of his temperance, and that, had he chanced to have a golden soul, he could not have applied to it a finer test. For that man, having accomplished so great a work and become for the Greeks the chief author of their freedom, and being reckoned all but greater than human, did not suffer the same thing as Pausanias, who set right the battle at Plataea; he was not lifted up by his deeds, nor grew insolent, nor thought any greater thoughts than before the battle. So orderly and decorous was he to the end. And yet Pausanias had not, surely, been the first to conquer the barbarians, but, looking to a pattern,

fought the battle at Marathon as his model; nor did he have the Lacedaemonians alone, as Miltiades had the Athenians, but with the Athenians themselves present and the rest of the Greeks, to whom this was agreeable; and indeed, since the Athenians there too accomplished most of the work along with the rest, they are said both to have destroyed the cavalry of the barbarians and to have prevailed over the Greeks ranged against them, and the assault on the wall fell wholly to them. But Miltiades did not then wait for the Lacedaemonians nor for any other men, nor did he share the work, but, having those from the city—save that some of the Plataeans, they say, came running to join—he made the danger his own, but the benefit common to all, being the first and only of the Greeks to conquer six-and-forty nations all together. So that it belonged to him to inscribe that he "destroyed the host of the Medes." For the work was, so to speak, his own. And what was earlier than this, the title "leader of the Greeks," fitted him exactly; for he began the freedom for all. Yet, even having done these things, he knew how to be temperate, and no one accused him of any such thing as Pausanias was much accused of. But we might find him given to factions and tumults, like Lysander, who did those wonderful deeds at Aegospotami and was thought to have brought down the war against the Athenians, but in truth began many great evils for the Greeks. But Miltiades neither did nor planned any such thing; he was, in a way, overcome by ambition, and at times overlooked the common advantage in seeking to advance his own friends—like

Agesilaus, who, being ambitious and devoted to his comrades beyond measure, took over the city of the Lacedaemonians when it ruled land and sea, and did not preserve it in that condition. And consider against whom I am measuring him: Lycurgus, Pausanias, Lysander, Agesilaus. But for these things no one could blame him; nor was he mastered by the pleasures of the body, as some have already accused Thibron the Spartan, and one might name countless others, both Greeks and barbarians. But—such are the native customs of democracy—to inform, to denounce, to confiscate, as in the case of Cleon and Cleophon and Hyperbolus and other men who were in no way orators (not, at least, if they were such men as that), but had received some phantom of rhetoric—if indeed one must call a phantom that which is in no way like the original, but in every way weaker. But he was clean of all these. How, then, was he not of advantage to the Greeks, being such a man? Or how did he not make men better, if anyone gave heed to him? These things follow of strong necessity. And if he was not learned in the heavenly bodies, like Anaxagoras—neither was Socrates wise in those matters, and that too though he had consorted with him, as they say. But Socrates was no worse than Anaxagoras—certainly not, as you yourselves would say—and so neither, perhaps, was Miltiades any worse than the sophists. And I think that even in a court of the gods Miltiades, were he tried, would be acquitted by every vote, not, as they say of Orestes, getting only half. And reasonably so; for the one slew his mother justly, but the other saved Greece justly, and paid the price of his rearing most nobly of all men, not only to his fatherland but also to the common nature of the Greek race. And indeed, city by city,

different men account different founders theirs, but one might justly hold that man to be the common founder of Greece. And for my part I think that even the charge he later incurred—if I must now say something about this too—is the greatest token that he far surpassed the rest. For all men thought it right to be overcome by his virtue, and that nothing was unconquered or untaken wherever Miltiades was present. Then am I to suppose that the man so brave and prudent and temperate, who through his whole life practiced virtue—that he gave himself over to some portion of flattery? The man who, even when he was on trial, showed the jurors nothing more than his wound, who did not weep, who did not lead his children up to the stand, though he had Cimon—am I to address this man so grandly as a flatterer? And was this the chief of all his policies and of his life: flattery? And how would one not justly accuse us ourselves of flattering and of doing the work of servants, not of free men, if, pursuing the favor of another, we willingly corrupt the truth? Indeed, to Plato we might grant many other things; but if we condemn him on these charges, I for one do not see what other honor we could render him. There remains, then, Themistocles—of all men the least deserving to hold the first place by descent from the second, even if it most clearly appears that this very thing belonged to him alone of all men. But rather it is perhaps a hard task to find who is second to him. For by so much did he surpass for us the man of Marathon, the famous one, the man—say it as

you like—by so much, then, did Themistocles surpass that man, beyond all who have come to my mind, by how much shall I say it admittedly?—by as much as Xerxes plainly surpassed Darius in all his preparations. And indeed the one conquered the king's satraps, the other the king himself; and after the battle of Marathon the king marched again, but after the sea-battle at Salamis he went off in flight. For by that defeat he was provoked, but by this one he gave up, so that he counted it sufficient gain if he should be saved. For he knew that the first time only a small part of his whole force had come, but now he was being defeated with almost all mankind. So neither did he himself have the heart to remain, nor did he send another thenceforth; for there was nothing he could hope for. Nay, even Mardonius, whom he left behind, he left as a man condemned to death, so to speak, and at the same time, as it seems to me, so that the Greeks might have someone to keep them occupied. For Miltiades, then, the demonstration of his courage came down to a single chief crisis, even though he employed it throughout his whole public life; but Themistocles was met by second tasks ever greater than the first, and the proverb came round upon him—for one wave left him only as another caught him up, until he came through the triple surges, conquering. And for Miltiades there was need of courage rather than wisdom for what was before him; but for Themistocles there was need of courage no less, if not even more, inasmuch as the fears too were greater; and besides this, he was answerable for many other qualities no less honorable that arose from the circumstances—understanding, indeed I might say a kind of divination, magnanimity, cleverness, mildness, endurance, adaptability to the occasions, to the affairs, to the men of the city, of Greece, and to the enemy. And it seems to me that what befell

Miltiades against the barbarians resembled rather a generalship, but that the work of Themistocles, when examined among all the Greeks, was precisely a statesmanship. So great were the things done and accomplished, some on land, some on sea; concerning which it seems to me that Homer too, had he survived and wished to speak of them, would have called upon the Muses no less than over how a single Thessalian ship was set on fire; or, if you like, over who was the first of the allies or of the Trojans themselves to stand against Agamemnon. Or rather, in that case he could not, I think, have learned who was the first to stand against the king of Asia and almost of Europe as well; but from what deeds and words he was able to accomplish these things, and against how many enemy ships and against what total armament and onset of the barbarian he drew up his line, and how human affairs then stood—this, it seems to me, he would ask and beg to be told, if even in small measure he were to lay hold of its worth. What, then, prevents us too now—and let our beginning be from the gods—from examining again how the state of the crisis stood, in the same way as we examined it just now, and showing in brief in what kind of circumstances Themistocles showed himself to be what kind of man? And yet this perhaps avails nothing. For things that cannot be set forth in speech—how could one behold that man from them? Unless one reflect on this very point: that matters concerning which it is not possible even to speak as one wishes, these that man handled as he wished. For ten years in succession the whole continent was in labor, all men contending to take vengeance for the battle of Marathon, and everything was being made ready out of every land and sea. And when Egypt revolted in the interval, the king, with no great effort, was again where he had been—so easily did he reduce it. But in the tenth year all the farthest peoples came together, and nations

all came, as if the inhabited world were migrating to another place; and the king set out, fearing that Greece might not contain the multitude—Greece, as it were a beginning of the whole earth—since his camp came to be wherever he wished, always. Gold and silver and bronze and iron, all were brought of equal worth, alike for land conveyances and for sea. And when the forces met at one point, the foot soldiers hid the coastline, and the ships hid the sea; and to the Greeks were reported—nothing worthy, indeed, of the evils that were coming, yet many things and of all kinds, such as had never been before. And the eclipse of the sun that occurred would not have so astounded them as the eclipse of land and sea that was taking place—owing, as it seems to me, rather to the king's desire than to his need. For he seemed truly to be sole master of land and sea, and to make and to destroy; for him Athos received the ships, and the Hellespont the foot soldiers. And besides this, walls were being built so that he might count his men by ten-thousands. And the sun was hidden by the arrows; the sea was full of ships, the land of foot soldiers, the air of missiles. To be present and to be at hand were one and the same, so that all were caught; everything shook as if Poseidon were coming down. Many of the nations were consumed for a single meal of the king. The threats of heralds did not cease as they went everywhere, demanding earth and water of whoever wished to be safe. And the oracle sent forth voices terrible and harsh to all the Greeks. They seemed likely to endure neither the rowing of the ships nor the noise of the horses. They could take courage neither in their sacrifices nor in their allies, nor even

find who among men might prove allies. And besides this, the one called Gelon would not give heed, the Argives held aloof, the Corcyraeans took counsel more cleverly than justly, the Thessalians, under compulsion indeed, yet were going over to the Mede; the Boeotians had fared no better than the Thessalians; the Delphians did not know what to do; and small was the sound part of Greece, and this hung upon two cities—or rather upon a single man, on whatever Themistocles should resolve or advise. In such crises, then, and in such an untimely confusion of all affairs, that man stood firm and was at no loss, nor was he dismayed, nor did he pray that the earth might swallow him, nor count blessed those long since dead, nor suffer the same thing as the many; rather he became for the Greeks like a good guardian spirit. For, taking everything upon himself and setting his own judgment in place of any other safeguard, and alone holding out with steady eyes against all things, both present and oncoming, and not turning away like those who look at the sun—which befell almost all men of that time—I would not say that he did not disappoint the hope of the Greeks, but rather that he far surpassed their expectation. For when the many thought they would suffer every extremity, and were looking to shameful contrivances and helpless refuges, he so changed the state of affairs that, if afterward, when the barbarians had departed, anyone had asked them whether they would have wished that those men had not marched against them, and that these things had not been done by them, and that the dangers had not befallen them nor the deeds been done, they would all

say they would rather die than have these things left undone by them. So far did he surpass not only the hopes of all who hoped the most among them, but even the prayers of the most part. And for my part I would gladly, if it were anyhow possible, ask Plato, by the gods of the Greeks: what ought Themistocles to have done in those times, or what to have said nobler than he said? Or what to have written better than he wrote? Or by what path of action to have proceeded? Or how to have led the Athenians? Or what better reckonings to have used? For tell me, by the gods—or, if not, let some other inherit the argument, let him speak, let him show—what Themistocles ought then to have done and how to have dealt with the circumstances. Should he have gathered the Athenians on the Pnyx and discoursed to them about the Forms, and taught them what justice-itself is, and what beauty-itself, and what that is which always is but has no becoming? Quickly, indeed, would becoming and being and everything else have failed them. Or should he have sought whence courage was first so named, and whence cowardice, and whether all things flow or not? They would have learned, indeed, that all things were flowing badly for them. But what, then, did he have to say or do at all? For this is the third question that has come round, like a watchword. From what shall we determine whether Themistocles was truly a counselor and leader and guide, or whether something else is the fitting name to hear? And indeed one of two things must be: either to be able to find fault with what was done by him, or to show what needful thing he left undone, having chosen the easier and pleasanter in place of the noble. And yet they say that the wisdom that comes after the event, and the reproaches made in safety, have nothing brilliant

nor lofty about them. I for one grant even this; and if anyone show a better action, or better words, or a juster choice, or one better for all than that which he established, as having then been possible, I am ready myself to inherit the blame. But if it is possible neither to find fault with any of his policies, nor to say of anything one might claim he ought to have done, that he did not do it, let us rather rejoice with ourselves in praising him than seek how to speak ill. Let us consider the matter in this way, bringing ourselves back to the facts themselves. There were three divisions of the Greeks: one outside the affairs—like the Argives and the Corcyraeans and the Sicilians and almost all the Italians, and the Cretans, indeed, and others, so they say; others actually joined in the march with the barbarians against Greece, like the Thessalians and all those up to Attica, save the Thespians and Plataeans, however many they were; and there remained a third, the Athenians and Lacedaemonians and as many as took refuge with them. But let it not yet be said that these were Athenians, nor that these prepared the rest. Rather, the whole Greek world was divided into so many parts, and the choice of these three lay in the midst before all, and both city and private man had to deliberate with regard to this; and the difference was not small—either, attaching themselves to the barbarian, to follow him against those who resisted; or to be allowed to keep quiet for themselves, having begged it, not to seek what would befall the others, but to count it gain if they themselves should suffer nothing; or, third, there was left to those who professed to care for the noble and the just, to contend against fire and sword and all things, and neither, though hearing, to hear the terrors, nor, though seeing, to see them, but, condemning all things as so much idle babble, to encamp beside death itself, judging this the extremity of life preferable for themselves rather than to concede anything unworthily. So be it. What, then, was it fitting the Athenians should choose then, or what should the counselor advise them? Here consider for me the resolutions of Themistocles.

"There the coward man and the valiant were made manifest"—not when we sit together in ambush, but when Greece stood upon the very razor's edge, whether to be or not to be. This is the first examination and trial of Themistocles. From here behold the man, beginning from the line; and bring me not gold in words, but apply the touchstone and consider. For remember your own image. The Athenians had to be among those contending for the common freedom, or to do one of the two remaining things. They had to be among the contenders. What then? Did Themistocles advise this, or hinder it? No—he was the very man who advised it. Was it not, then, this that they had to do, and this to advise? This the Athenians did, and Themistocles advised it. Up to this point, then, he advised the greatest things, and Plato has nothing to charge him with; nay, unless he praise him brilliantly, I do not think he could fail to be ashamed. For not only does he plainly bring the Athenians to these things and station them in this resolve, but the other Greeks too, so far as they shared in the affairs, this one man above all strengthened and spurred on, and persuaded them—some willing, some unwilling—to become good and profitable to themselves; he who even gave such answers to the heralds who came from the king concerning earth and water that it was possible for all the Greeks to learn what kind of answers one must give to the barbarians who come for such purposes. And he did not stop his freedom there, but killed even the interpreter, accusing him of having lent his voice, like any other instrument, to the Persian against the Greeks. And yet what terrible thing was it for the Athenians to learn what was being said, and, having learned, to deliberate? For he did not himself

propose it, nor compel them. But still he did not think fit to serve even so far, since it was not even proper to hear such things. Quickly indeed would he himself have served, who treated his servants thus—or have spoken before the people against what he thought best, who would not even allow the interpretation of matters about which it was not better to speak. Such, then, were the preludes of the public life of Themistocles and of the contest for freedom—nothing like those of Meles the citharode, nor like the songs Plato says that man sang, but rather the opposite. For both what is best is in them, and what is sweetest is added for every noble and free man to hear. So that to me it seems liker to the music of Terpander, except that it even surpassed it. For he brought one city, that of the Lacedaemonians, into harmony, but this man tuned and held together all Greece—for I call Greece those who were able to come to the aid of all Greece—and he became the leader of so much greater and more common a concord, one that extended further. First, then, he put an end to the wars that were then standing in Greece and to the differences and factions of all toward one another, and persuaded them to count one war alone, that against the barbarians, but themselves friends and kinsmen. Then, those of the citizens who had been exiled he advised the Athenians to bring back—among whom were some at variance with him—preserving the same judgment in matters both Greek and within the city; and this judgment was to look to the common good, putting away all pettiness of soul. Having taken over affairs, then, and become the leader of the whole danger, what kind of man did he show himself, both in understanding what was needful and in carrying it through to the end? Such that, if anyone were asked whatever the question, what it was that saved the affairs of the Greeks, he would not be left to inquire, but it would be possible for all at once to say

that first the gods, and then, so far as it came to men, one city, that of the Athenians, and the judgment of one man, that of Themistocles. For seeing that, unless someone should conquer the barbarians with the fleet, Greece would be undone city by city, as they attacked all in turn and ravaged them, and besides this knowing too that affairs on land had far more and more terrible difficulties, and that they would fight against far more and harder enemies than by sea, he chose first the lesser extremity in place of the greater; and then, where he should use daring at the right moment. And these things the god at Delphi confirmed by vote. Yet even when the oracle came, there was perplexity for the many as to what this "wooden wall" could be. So the old men advised holding to the acropolis—so far did they rave, for it had of old been fenced with a thorn-hedge, and they took the oracle to refer to this. And the oracle-mongers chanted everything, except that one thing of all they did not chant, namely that they must fight at sea. Nay, they advised guarding against Salamis above all—the very same men who once urged on the expedition to Sicily; for I call the same kind one and the same breed, except, of course, that the ones speaking for Alcibiades came later, while these spoke against Themistocles then—and on the whole they thought it best to seek something else, and, fleeing outside Greece, to settle another land. But in the end it was resolved by the Athenians to let the oracle-chanters be, and rather to trust Themistocles, who interpreted the wooden wall to be the triremes, and that something good lay stored up in Salamis,

wherefore the god had addressed it as divine; since, if some evil were going to seize the Greeks in it, the address of it would be "wretched," not "divine." But in fact it referred to the barbarians, that many of them would perish. They must therefore fight at sea. And these things, reasonably, the others found hard to put together, but Themistocles found easy to discover. For it was not when the oracles came that he first held this opinion, nor was he improvising, nor had he become wise in this wisdom on the occasion, like the prophets of god; rather, even before the Athenians sent to Delphi and before the barbarian stirred, that man long since and from afar had considered and seen these things, and had taken forethought that, on the occasion and at the time of need, he should not be at a loss. For when much money had accrued to the city from the works of the silver mines, and this was about to be distributed at random, he alone of all dared to oppose it, doing the work not of a servant, nor of one ministering to desires, nor of one filling up pleasures, but rather, as it seems to me, of a counselor and teacher—willingly passing over the pleasantest, but foreseeing and doing the best, even if it must cause pain; imitating the physician, not the cook—or rather the trainer too, as you would say—since before the danger and the hardships he did what was advantageous, and so that affairs should not give way under the Greeks. He bade the Athenians, then, to disregard the distribution, and to build ships out of the money, on the pretext of the war against the Aeginetans (for this was then at hand), but in truth foreseeing what was to come and thinking that the battle of Marathon had been, as it were, a prelude for the Athenians, and was not the end of the whole war nor its conclusion, but rather a beginning and a preparation for other greater contests. And saying these things at the outset he persuaded them, and the triremes were built; and then he persuaded them that they must use the triremes and attend to the sea, since they had no better base of operations for the war against the barbarians. And first, sailing to

Artemisium, he set up two trophies for two sea-battles, neither, I think, having spoken unseemly words to the Athenians or Greeks who sailed with him, nor having displayed mean deeds, but, as Pindar says, having laid for the Greeks the foundation of freedom. Then he wrote that decree, than which none more wonderful or more freedom-loving is recorded as ever having been written. But I seem to be passing over many things between; better, perhaps, to go back. For so truly was that man born, by some divine portion, on behalf of all Greece, and saw nothing better than the common advantage, that when the Greeks had gathered to one place, the Athenians surpassed almost all in the number of their ships, yet, since the Greeks were more inclined toward the Lacedaemonians and willing that they should lead, that man, best in all things, perceiving that, if he should examine the just claim precisely and a faction should arise over the leadership, all would perish miserably and they would have no resource, persuaded the Athenians to yield and concede the leadership for the time to the Lacedaemonians, promising that he would recover it for them from the willing Greeks. And he did not deceive them; he persuaded them to give up almost the name of the leadership, but not the leadership itself, since, if the truth be told, they assigned to themselves the leadership but to those others the title, and there resulted for them, besides the common safety, the prevailing over the enemy by courage and over the allies by mildness, and a bearing in every way nobler and more august; for they became leaders of leaders. And if you say, Plato, that cities have no need of triremes or dockyards, but of good counsel and

temperance, Themistocles not only found the triremes for the Athenians—nor, what is greater than this, used them on behalf of the common rights and for the need of all the Greeks—but he himself also brought to the cities and accomplished that good concord, which saved Greece no less than the ships themselves; or rather, he made it possible to use the ships themselves. And what I said a little before is here finely shown: by how much the man was greater than Terpander in music. For the one made the Lacedaemonians of one mind among themselves, but the other then persuaded both Athenians and Lacedaemonians to be of one mind—or rather, persuaded all the Greeks to become of a single judgment; so well and nobly did he attune Greece, and himself withdrew from the command of the fleet and persuaded the others to the leadership, though they so far surpassed and were alone a hope for affairs. And yet what greater proof of temperance and endurance did any of those who have rotted away in their threadbare cloaks ever produce? Yet, as he gave up the bearing, so he did not give up the forethought concerning affairs, as I said, nor did he yield to any city or any man, but he himself advised all things, as if he were sole leader of all, and went on adorning and shielding and instructing beforehand Eurybiades, the admiral of the Lacedaemonians, like a child—as those who hold up by their own hands men unable to swim—not exposing him, but, as it were, coaxing him with the title of the command, since that he himself was admiral and master of all, and that it was for him, the very admiral, to turn things wherever he wished, he showed throughout the whole command, and indeed then at once. For when Eurybiades was struck with consternation at the multitude of the barbarian triremes—some of which he saw bearing straight against him, and others he heard were sailing around—and was minded to abandon the contest, not on any better hope, but, as happens in such cases, counting it gain to ward off the present danger, suffering such a

passion and looking toward the Peloponnese, that man himself, like some god from the machine, stretched out his hand and prevented affairs from being ruined when they had begun from so shameful a beginning; and Eurybiades, when he could not persuade him by speaking, he bought—not as though deeming himself worthy to be anyone's servant, but rather using that man as a servant; and he both saved Euboea and set the affairs of the Greeks so that they were not utterly without resource, having afforded them, once they made trial, ground to trust. And when the disaster at Thermopylae was announced, and when the common prophecy—if it is right to say so—both of Pythian Apollo and of Themistocles had now for the second time become manifest, that everything lay in the ships—for both those who entered Thessaly to guard Tempe, betrayed by whomsoever it was, withdrew, and those who went to meet the enemy at Thermopylae were overwhelmed by the barbarians; and one can say not only so much about them, but that the Lacedaemonians too seem to me, having known this from the beginning, as if making expiation toward the Greeks, to have sent off only as many as they could bear to be deprived of, since failure was to be expected—when, then, things had gone thus, and those in the ships were now fleeing with all their might to within Greece, and were almost making the Peloponnese into Greece,

while abandoning the rest, he withdrew last with the last of the Athenians, not keeping the same rank as when it was time to sail out; for then he was first among the first. And if again you wish here too the by-work of the road—what policy he pursued toward the Ionians, not from the platform, nor seen by them, but from the rocks and the anchorages where he hoped to encounter them—what Homeric Minos could find fault with this, or what Aeacus lifting his hands on behalf of the Greeks to Zeus? Here, then, the third trial, much greater and nobler, came upon him, since the triremes carried everything, and to expect anything else was vain. For when the Greeks had withdrawn from Artemisium, the Athenians even so both made their own preparations and bade the others come to meet them in Boeotia and to take the first risk on behalf of the rest of Greece; but the others came to such a pitch of helplessness—for it is not right to call it treachery—that they did not have the heart to go out, but, fortifying across the Isthmus from sea to sea, they did much as if, wrapping themselves up, they were handing themselves over. For where it was possible for the barbarians, sailing around, to take them city by city, what good was the wall, even if it had been raised more august than that of the Babylonians and stronger than every contrivance? Therefore, with the Athenians left alone and the rest of the Greeks toiling to no profit, it remained for everything to be seized in silence, both by land and by sea. These things Themistocles, foreseeing from afar, was not dismayed at then; but when the barbarians were now pouring in from both sides, both the ships approaching in a common

armada and the foot soldiers bursting into Boeotia, and the fire burning everything and signaling, in place of beacon-fires, that the king was advancing, he wrote that decree: to entrust the city to Athena, guardian of Athens; to convey the children and women to Troezen, and the old men to Salamis, and that the rest, embarking on the triremes, should contend for freedom. O the great and prodigious conception, and the wonderful strength of him who first hoped to persuade these things and did not despair of so great a matter! And wonderful too was the virtue and discipline of those who were persuaded—the discipline in which they had been trained under him, to endure and bear up under everything that the divine power should grant and Themistocles advise. This decree is the noblest and most brilliant and most perfect witness under the sun in the reckoning of virtue, holding in succession a demonstration of all the best things: of taking courage in the gods, of having confidence in themselves, of being willing to suffer anything before making trial of anything shameful, and, besides these, of guarding the resolutions made from the beginning, of bearing no grudge against their like, even if they seem to have chosen the deeds of unlike men. This decree, it seems to me, no flatterer composed, nor a man with downcast eyes, nor one fawning on his hearers, but some one of the gods uttered through the tongue of Themistocles. Surely Mithaecus, who wrote the treatise on Sicilian cookery, or Sarambus the tavern-keeper—for now I have recalled the name—

do you think composed these things? Come, then, set beside this decree the writings of the sophists, if you like, and the laws—for I have no need to name them. And I think it would appear of less worth than not many of them. And yet it was the part of a servant, and of one pursuing the favor of the moment, above all to render service in what the many commanded; or, failing that, guessing at their mind, to say and do what he supposes will be to their pleasure, or at least to deviate a little from their desire. But Themistocles was so far from doing these things and conducting his policy with a view to the desire and pleasure of the many that, though he saw them weeping, and heard children and women lamenting, and besides some being left behind of necessity, and the whole thing being most like as if the city had been taken by storm—and reasonably so; for the future was for all in obscurity, holding a thin and untrustworthy hope, but the present was the loss of city and possessions and the whole former way of life, and not even to travel the same road, nor to settle in the same place, but to be torn apart, parents and children and wives and husbands, and everything was most dreadful to hear, let alone to endure; so that even the tame dogs, they say, howled at the abandonment, and the other beasts followed down to the sea, and there was great confusion—seeing and hearing all this, the most enduring of all men held firm—things which what kind of Odysseus, seeing his wife, could easily have borne without tears?—and taking them like children he led them out with an untroubled soul and reckonings that stood firm, not only in his eyes, as though leading them out to some procession, or as colonists, and not leading them to Salamis. And they

were persuaded, and, leaving behind temples and tombs and land, looked to Themistocles alone, preferring him to children and parents and the necessities of nature, and clinging to his voice as to a sacred anchor. Not even Orpheus could then have drawn them over to himself. And indeed all that he continued to say and do in Salamis, now conducting his policy among all the Greeks, and how many and what kind of utterances he sent forth on behalf of the noble and the just, and how many contests he carried through and with what affairs he was beset, whenever he had to persuade men, contending again from the beginning over the same matters; and the company he kept with Aristides, the man surnamed best of the Greeks and most just, and how they vied with one another in their dealings, and how he was not far behind in the exchanges; and the "Strike, but hear," uttered to Eurybiades beyond anything of Socrates, and countless other things—it would be endless to tell. And when no one contradicted him, but they did not dare to remain, and the words were poured out in fear, and flight was prevailing, and the most shameful things were about to come to pass—and not merely the matter of slavery, but first to run away, then to be enslaved, and to seem to the barbarians bad slaves before becoming slaves—then, then indeed, beyond all physicians who save against compulsion and against the patient's distaste, he brought the barbarians upon them

having deceived both sides—the one as though summoning them out of goodwill, the other as though he knew nothing of the matter; so that Aristides was good in bringing him word—and, having taken them and brought down the third and greatest of all falls, I think, and the most complete, he cast out Xerxes as a fugitive from the farthest borders of Attica, and moreover told him to flee. And the king, as though serving a master, obeyed his orders, and when bidden to pursue the Greeks he hearkened, and when commanded to flee he was persuaded, and besides he was grateful; and he who before gave orders to others against the Greeks was then compelled to listen to one of the Greeks—and that the most hated and most hostile of all. So much, it seems, did Themistocles surpass in mastery over service. Therefore, in choosing war in place of inaction, he displayed a mark of courage; and in choosing to make war against the barbarians on behalf of the Greeks, rather than against the Greeks alongside the barbarians, a mark at once of courage and of justice—choosing the fewer in place of the more and greater, and his own kin in place of the foreign. And further, by his finding out what was needful and foreseeing it and being nowhere deceived in affairs, but foretelling the future better than the prophets, he reasonably won a reputation for wisdom; and by his corrupting none of what he had resolved through the pleasures of the body, but ever giving himself leisure for the best things and attending to the reasonings concerning the leadership, and by his restraining the Athenians concerning the leadership, and in all these things—surely no one can be temperate who does not assign to that man the first place in temperance. Can

any of you who practice philosophy without risk give such a pledge of virtue, or, having passed through so many tests, claim to do so? And I think that on both sides, and beside both, Themistocles stands—both Miltiades and Cimon. For he plainly was the first to conquer the barbarians by sea, as Miltiades by land. So that he might reasonably seem to have begun the freedom in this respect too, and he plainly added to what already existed. For to the land-battle he added the sea-battles, and set up three trophies in place of one, just as Cimon went on to the second tasks. And indeed he took over the Greeks neither in the same security in which Cimon found them, nor in the same fears as Miltiades, but faring at the very extremity of extremities, in the first and last of dangers; in a word, he was the first and only to conquer the king himself, household and all, not as Miltiades conquered the satraps first at Marathon, and Pausanias later at Plataea. One might call the battle of Marathon a paradigm and honor it for its priority in time, but reckon the deeds of Themistocles in and by themselves, as done later in time than the battle of Marathon, yet having had their beginning at home, from that man's understanding and statesmanship. For nothing comparable had been done before by the Greeks—nay, had not even been hoped. Thus he surpasses both Miltiades and Pausanias and Cimon; and he becomes the equal of three—not of a baker and a cook and a tavern-keeper, but of men who had become something to the

Greeks. And he alone, indeed, plainly conquered both the land force and the naval force by right reasoning. For neither did the ships hold out, and the king departed in flight together with the greater part. And by however much one exalts the later victory at Plataea, by so much the more does he adorn the understanding and forethought of that man. For if a small fraction of the land force, left behind, nevertheless caused the Greeks trouble—and that too when paradigms now stood before them both by land and by sea—by how much it is fitting that they be superior to the barbarians, and moreover when it was a satrap of the king, not the king himself, who remained—then surely no one would have recognized the fire-bearer contending against all and not against a part, when the king was set over affairs, when no one, in the present circumstances, was at hand on whom they might take courage, when the army was advancing untouched by ills and with hopes undiminished, exalted by the deed at Thermopylae, and all but holding it before their eyes that all these too must soon lie dead. But all this the "service" and "flattery" of Themistocles, as Plato says, but, as the common vote of the Greeks holds, the wisdom and forethought of Themistocles, prevented, and imposed order on all the deeds. So that not only from what he set right when himself leading, but from what he was the cause of others setting right in the matters that came to them—as for Pausanias, for Cimon, for the rest—he would justly meet with the good repute of all. Or

we should do utter wrong, Plato, if we should not dare to deem worthy of even one of the fair words a man who showed such humane deeds toward the Greeks. To me, then, Themistocles seems to have become no meaner nor less honorable in commanding the Athenians than Socrates in serving in the ranks at Delium and at Amphipolis and at Potidaea. And yet you praise that man because, in the retreat from Delium, he went off courageously, and was plainly seen to be one who, if anyone laid hold of him, would defend himself well and nobly. Is it not, then, terrible—O earth and gods and leaders of words and deeds, for I am carried away to speak—to praise Socrates even for his flight, and to declare that he retreated more nobly than Laches, but, of Themistocles, who displayed his courage by pursuing and not fleeing the enemy, and of whose virtue all Greece enjoyed the benefit, to take no thought of calling him by names that belong to cowardice and unmanliness? Of him who, even when he withdrew victorious from Euboea, accomplished in the meantime such things as no one in any haste to depart would ever do. And then you say that safety is not worth much. What, then, prevents us from saying that even to the savior gods, who save us one by one, those men afforded for the Greeks the accomplishing of those things?—But I will let the blasphemy go; one may, however, suspect what follows from the argument. For my part, I would think that argument better and more just, and that one would not err in speaking thus: that the gods are in truth saviors, and these men are those who then saved Greece, but that Miltiades and Themistocles served as ministers—which is the greatest and noblest

power of a human being, to serve the higher powers. This, then, divine head, is the right thing to say; and I too would declare that those men became ministers and servants—not of the people of the Athenians, far from it, nor of any men at all, unless one must call presiding and commanding "serving" and "ministering." Moreover, then, one would not even allow us, by these arguments, to feel gratitude to our parents, nor to set it down to the account of benefaction, who afforded us the beginnings of living and being saved. And if one should bring in Euripides too as a witness, saying that "we ought, gathering in assembly, to lament the newborn for all the evils to which he comes," he would seem, surely, to say something very much to the point. But I think that, of the circumstances in which we find ourselves, and of living worse or better, we hold the daemon and fortune to blame—and, by Zeus, if you like, add that we ourselves too must bear a share, for there is no harm to the argument—but to those who ministered to our coming-to-be, and through whom we first came into the light, to these we think we must hold the first and greatest gratitude, after the gods who are still prior to them. If, then, to our parents, for the mere fact of existence, we hold such gratitude and confess that we owe a debt the most venerable of all debts, how can it be that Miltiades and Themistocles must not be thought to have done something more, who became for the Greeks the cause not only of living and of safety, but accustomed them to be better instead of worse in the very things they did? It seems to me absurd that, if they had betrayed some allies or a fort, or one or two ships, or had been the cause to any of exile or death, men would drive them with many and frequent reproaches and enroll them with Eurybatus and Phrynondas—as he has called Archelaus wretched, surely, and miserable, for killing those whom he ought not—but, since they freed all men both by land and by sea,

taking the first risk, and saved not only the bodies and the souls of those who entrusted themselves to them, but also cities and country and polity and customs and laws and the very name of the race, and left nothing whatever of courage and justice undone, but handed over Greece greater than they received it, and brought away to the gods the fitting thank-offerings for these things, and passed their lives, so to speak, keeping festival both in their deeds and in their policies, and established before all men their own virtue, which they held toward both gods and men—that we should think it right to deem them of the portion of Mithaecus and Thearion; and to say that physicians are better than cooks because they save, but to liken those who presided over the safety of the Greeks not to physicians but to cooks! And indeed, even if they made no one better but saved them, this at least was a thing physicians do, not cooks. So that they were in no way worse than physicians. How, then, were they of no worth to the Greeks? Plato himself would not concede this to himself. Elsewhere, at least, where there is no contentiousness, he says this; and he says it on behalf of the Sicilian men, in arranging a kind of royal rule for them, as though Dion himself, being of the line of which his ancestors were, says that they at least saved, which is the greatest thing, the Greeks from the barbarians, so that it is now possible to make speeches about polity; but, had they perished then, neither speech nor hope would have been left anywhere at all by any means.

Therefore in these words he praises those who became the cause of safety for the Greeks, and says that thanks must be paid them—and not mean thanks, but such as one would not easily even ask for oneself—and to the man who is displeased he says that "the ancestors saved the greatest thing, the Greeks, from the barbarians." Either, then, it was fitting to erase that, or these things have been refuted by those. For it is not possible to say that, while it is reasonable that thanks and gifts belong to those who saved the Greeks in Sicily, yet to those who saved all the ancient Greece, and, by the same path of statesmanship, Sicily and Italy and the Greeks wherever on earth and sea they are, to these there should be no share even of a humane word, nor should it be possible for them even to be called good men. And indeed you yourself say that you care no more for those in Cyrene than for those at Athens. Then, having allowed their descendants to speak about gifts, you thought it right to speak ill of the men themselves, and at once both refute the tyrants and blame those who were the cause of freedom for the Greeks. And here is the crown of the argument: that not even freedom is anything very august, but that for many it is better to obey others than to be free. Very well. Was it then better, also at that time, for the Athenians to obey? And indeed, not from afar, but from the very things they did, they showed themselves worthy of freedom. Moreover, it was no Dioscuri, nor Theseus son of Poseidon, nor Heracles the common champion of all, nor the best and most just of the demigods, that there was danger of obeying, but men full of insolence and evils, from whom they were likely to learn no good thing

whatever, but to suffer all the most shameful and most terrible things. So that how would it not have come to the most shameful of all situations, if, having earlier rescued the Heraclids into freedom, they had then themselves bowed beneath the barbarians, accounting the matter of small worth? But indeed, if they themselves were not worthy to be slaves, nor were the invaders better than they, and the danger, for those overcome, concerned the very extremities, how was this not, if anywhere, the occasion to show themselves more afraid of slavery than of death? For I will add the very words of Plato. And if this was known to everyone, and to all these things were best and most serious and the only things—come, if the truth must be told—belonging to the better argument and to political virtue brought to its extremity, how can those who afforded themselves to these things and secured for all, together with safety, their freedom, be thought of little worth either to the citizens or to the Greeks? And indeed they did not even make their freedom unbridled; for, while toward the barbarians they were so disposed as to be unwilling even to hear a voice, toward the Greeks they were so common and humane that they willingly yielded the leadership to the Lacedaemonians, though they so far surpassed them. And therefore they recovered it again from the willing Greeks. So that it was not without justice nor without temperance, Plato, that they filled the city with allies and tribute and idle babble, as you say, but, beginning from a temperate and just and wonderful rule, they guarded most nobly the bounds of freedom, leading the citizens midway between arrogance and lowliness, and not introducing the dissolute freedom, nor what one might offhand call freedom, but that which goes with justice and temperance.
