And indeed, that to free one's fatherland—to say nothing of Greece—is no dishonorable thing, nor the work of any chance man, Plato himself is witness, or, if you like, Dion; since this too is part of that speech: "And upon all these things, with guileless and sound judgment, together with the gods, set up as king first my son, for the sake of two favors: that from me and that from my father. For the one freed the city from the barbarians in that time, and I from tyrants now twice over, of which you yourselves have been witnesses." Does Plato, then, set it down as a small or mean thing to make a city free, or to prevent one about to belong to others? Since, then, it is right to give even kingship in return for this, and that too to one's descendants, and all but to yield freedom itself to them, because their ancestors guarded freedom—then surely, that those who freed not only the citizens but the whole race of the Greeks should not be allowed even to share in the very appearance of being free, is one of the most terrible things; but that men should rob of its due portion of freedom those who in deed preserved that freedom for the others. Come, then, let us consider this too: by how much in this respect also Miltiades and Themistocles were more just than Dion and better in matters of state and more careful to preserve equality, seeing that they, in return for those deeds, asked nothing more either for themselves or for their children, but supposed it enough to have benefited the Greeks; while Dion, as you say, needed even such gifts as included that the rest should obey those of his line—not, on each occasion nor in the affairs themselves, being persuaded that these reasoned or spoke better than the rest, but once for all setting up kings, even if some among them were better. Have you not on every side convicted yourself? Seeing that even of equality and of geometry those men plainly are thus mindful, but Dion not, nor the children of Dion, and that too though

they had consorted with Plato, the man most terrible at geometry. And third, the letter says, one must summon the man who now commands the army of the enemy, Dionysius son of Dionysius, to become king of Syracuse willingly, the city being willing—if he is willing willingly to pass over into the form of a king—fearing the turns of fortune, and pitying his fatherland and the neglect of the temples and the tombs, lest through contentiousness he should utterly destroy everything and become a delight to the barbarians. If, then, even for the tyrant's son and the commander of the enemy's army there is a fitting occasion to be reconciled, if he is willing to become king instead of tyrant, pitying his fatherland and the neglect of temples and tombs, then surely with the benefactors of the Greeks, and through whom temples and tombs and all things were saved and Greece did not become a delight to the barbarians, it would have been reasonable to make a treaty, and to remit even the blasphemy against them, even if he had nothing more to assign them in deed. For come, by the gods—if, when those affairs were at hand, Themistocles, when the Athenians summoned him and bade him aid them with whatever he had, had asked nothing else, neither tyranny nor lawful kingship, but only this much—that he should not be called a servant by them, nor receive such a reproach, if he should set their affairs in order—had Plato been present, what would he have advised the Athenians—he who advised these things to the Syracusans? Would he not have thought the challenge of Themistocles moderate and have granted the favor? For to me it seems he would even have pledged himself for these things on behalf of his fatherland. Is it not, then, absurd that, while the deeds were still going to be, and as to how they should be done, he should pledge only this on behalf of all, but, when they have come to pass and been done and that man's virtue has become manifest to all Greeks and barbarians, nevertheless to attempt to insult him, and to be ashamed neither before temples nor tombs nor inscriptions, but to speak ill of one whom, had a man wished to praise him, it would have been a task to reach his worth? And indeed it is not the same thing to speak, in the midst of the sea, about those in the

boat and to display one's own good courage, and to sit outside the storm beneath the little wall—which Plato, knowing better than anyone, willingly passes over, and accuses Themistocles of embarking the Athenians on the triremes, not in these words but elsewhere, saying that they were accustomed by this to flee and not to fight standing their ground. As though you and I had routed many companies of hoplites, but Themistocles knew nothing but to flee! Yet I, if it had been possible to conquer in some other way, or even to be saved at first, would perhaps think these words had something in them; but when the choice was either to prevail by fighting at sea, or to perish on land, how was it equal, or what is the wonderful philosophy of dying in vain when it was possible to be saved with the greatest glory? In the first place, for my part I do not conceive where it has been determined that to conquer by land is noble, but by sea shameful; or that the cornel-wood and the hide are worth much, but the ship-timbers and the oar-handles worth nothing—as if one should remove the sea from the things that are, or say it came into being in vain, and strike out the realm of Poseidon, which holds second place among all things, as Homer says. Why, then, shall we not also accuse them concerning their grain, that they use mostly imported grain and have further need of the sea, when it is possible to be content with the country they farm, O most divine of men?—This means perishing by famine. And indeed, if the bringing in of grain by sea is for them necessary and saving, for the sake of the same safety they then too made use of the sea, and the portion of the noble was added to the need. And indeed neither is it possible to say that the grain had to come to them by sea, but that one need not foresee how they would be masters of the grain-convoy. Therefore there was need of triremes and of knowing how to fight at sea. How, then, was he who advised these things a busybody, or how did he not adapt himself to the nature of the country, that we may add this too? And we should seem to me to be doing the like, if we should make these accusations, as if we found fault even with the nature of Attica,

that the sea surrounds it almost entirely. What, then, if it seemed thus good to the higher powers? But still I let these things go for Plato's sake. Let the neighborhood be briny, as he says. If, then, Themistocles exchanged victory for victory, did he wrong the shipwrights in honoring them in place of the spear-makers? And yet the work of the sea-battle came down, surely, to the hoplites on the decks—of whom we must think the greater part were among those who risked themselves at Marathon. And if then they took on a double danger instead of a single one—the one against the enemy, the other against the sea itself—they are, I think, in no way the worse for this. But I for my part take away even these additions. Let it be wholly a fault, if there was any other means of safety for their affairs. But if all the land had been seized, and the army was flowing in like an inundation of the sea, and everything was being utterly snatched away, and there was no looking up, but some willingly joined the enemy, others were led unwillingly, and others kept fleeing ever to within Greece, and the Athenians alone were left outside; and besides this, they called even then, when affairs were in this state, on those in the alliance, and bade them, coming together with them into Boeotia, to take the first risk on behalf of the rest, but no one obeyed—rather they sat in the straits not only of the Peloponnese but also of their hopes; and it was destined to be nowhere, neither of land nor of sea—why do we judge these Achaeans from the tower? Or why do we accuse things that nowhere come to pass? For my part, I do not think the sea-battle at Salamis holds so much shame that it would have been more choiceworthy to perish before it; rather, beyond the life and the safety belonging to that time, I would call this, as it were, a gain that befell those of that time—to accomplish so great a deed and to set up a trophy common to all men, so to speak, and for all time. For they seem to me not only to have conquered their adversaries on that day, nor only the Greeks present, but also

to have surpassed all men in greatness of daring and in the majesty of their victory. For if one must say one thing out of all that has come to memory, one would justly call that deed the greatest. And Themistocles seems to me alone of all men, or at least among a very few, to have shown that the saying is true which long ago Alcaeus the poet uttered, and which afterward the many took up and used—that cities are not stones nor timbers nor the craft of builders, but wherever there are men who know how to save themselves, there are walls and cities. Therefore, by the truest of arguments, he did not think he was abandoning the city, but rather refitting it, as on a stage, to meet the present circumstance; for not even in the dramas does any of the competitors destroy his own nature, if for the present he changes his costume; and at that time it fell to the Athenians to put on the bearing of seafaring men and to show the city in this. For these reasons he gave up the country and the very soil of the city, but preserved its dignity most nobly of all men, and gave up walls and hearths and temples before the post of his high spirit and the things of which he had convinced himself. For he knew that, if he clung to those things and clung to life for their sake, he would quickly be deprived even of them and would destroy the men themselves besides and cast away all hopes at once; but if he should put the ships before them and stand aside for the very time of the decision, like some competitor going abroad for the sake of prizes, he easily hoped that, just as then he chose the sea in place of the land, so again out of the sea he would find both the country and the city and would use things in no way worse. And reflecting on these things he imitated the runners who from far off catch up those ahead; and, having yielded not only Attica but the whole land to Xerxes and allowed him to seize it first, but having taken so much of the sea as sufficed for the ships, he overturned for him all his hopes, and

rescued Greece—not accustoming the Athenians to be sailors instead of hoplites, nor finding for them in the triremes a provision for flight, nor that they should dwell on the sea for all time, like Glaucus of Anthedon, they say, or Saron who gave his name to the gulf, but the very opposite, O wonderful sir, that nevertheless they should fear no multitude of enemies nor flee, but, even if they must give up all the land, even if they must withdraw from their very bodies, should easily endure it for the sake of the higher good, and should not be slaves to their possessions nor count any pretext sufficient for becoming worse—neither a multitude of enemies, nor strength, nor that all men had consented to be slaves, nor that everything was turned upside down—but should hold both the sea more their own and every danger more endurable than living with shame. This is a good paradigm both for hoplites and for cavalry and for archers and for crews of triremes and for all the complements of a city. One must not, he says, give one's back to the enemy nor seek a shameful safety, nor, casting aside the reckonings concerning what is just, give oneself over to him who would carry one off, nor flee that one may not fight. "I, at least," he says, "did not go off in flight to Italy, nor did I think it right to found a city there, though the prophets bade me, but I remained with the triremes, where it was the time to range myself on behalf of Greece. And when the things on land had been seized, a small part of the sea sufficed me; and I counsel you too," he says, "to remain and keep your post, whether you contend in a contest of hoplites, or of cavalry, or of any kind whatever. But if you are even shut out of everything, become for me a man of the sea

for this time; here be a hoplite, hold out your shield from the ship, and, if it is possible, even from the very sea bear it over the surge." These things Themistocles taught, and this was the meaning of his moving the city onto the triremes; for these reasons he thought it right to make the country empty of men rather than that any captured man in it should be a slave. Than these there have come to be no nobler reasonings, nor deeds more honorable, nor any holding together more fully understanding and magnanimity and courage. Since that he did not at all think fit to disregard the city utterly, nor to flee in a circle on the triremes, but supposed that these things were advantageous for the present occasions, and, having used Salamis as a camp in the same way the earlier men used Marathon, again was mindful of the original things, he showed before long. For when the barbarians had departed, he led them up at once into the city and resettled it as before, and even extended the circuit wider, as the interpreters say, on every side; and when there was need to wall it, he alone of all found out how they would be able. How, then, did he accustom them to flee, or by what stroke of fortune—he who accustomed them, when in the utmost dangers, to pursue, not to flee, but, when they had conquered and were faring most prosperously and it was possible for them to take whatever country and city they wished, led them back to the old places and did not allow them to be unmindful of what they had? By Zeus, Plato—if someone, laying hold of you, accused you, saying how much sea you sailed across in merchant ships, and how great a wandering you wandered about Charybdis, encamped together with the sailors and in need of the oar and the oar-loop, and that too though you so disliked things of the sea and were attached to the hoplites—would you not, indeed, since you are a man of the Muses and have long since condemned the phrase—the kind I mean—decline to say, O

"wretch, you are mad," but would have said somewhat thus: "My good man, I did these things not because I had chosen the life of the sailors, nor adorning them in place of the hoplites, nor learning anew to go to sea in my old age, nor harming the affairs of the mainland, but it was not otherwise possible to come to Sicily"? These things, I think, you would be able to say—just as we say on behalf of Themistocles, that it was not otherwise possible for the Greeks to be saved. And indeed no one would say that, for the affairs of Dion, one had to sail to Sicily and reckon neither old age nor danger nor having been often deceived nor anything else against the just claim and the need of that man; but, for the sake of Greece and of such great affairs, one need not have used the ships, but should have refused the sea. No one would say so. And Bellerophon, my excellent friend, as the poets say, mastered the Chimaera not by embarking on the sea, but by mounting into the air upon Pegasus, and yet was not thought to be a coward—he who was even thought able to destroy whole companies. But, I think, against the fire it was not possible to hold out from the ground. And I know about Themistocles that, even if he had been able to imitate Daedalus and, having winged himself, to assail the barbarian on behalf of the Greeks, he would not have shrunk even from this; or, if, about to join a battle on foot, he had advanced from the higher ground, he would not on that account have been likely to incur the charge of cowardice. And the Lacedaemonians—you yourself say that, fighting the battle at Plataea, they were unwilling to stand their ground, but drew the Persians toward what was advantageous to themselves. For I pass over the Scythians, and how many victories they have won by fleeing. Where a man thinks he will have the advantage, there let him ward off the enemy, especially if he transgress none of the greater rights. If, then, Themistocles had used his own judgment alone concerning these matters, one might say he had brought the accusation upon himself; but since a god too

plainly ordained these things, I for my part hesitate to speak, but everyone would understand the rest. Themistocles, then, brilliantly escapes the charge. Or, by the gods themselves—when it is needful that Socrates should seem wisest, shall we refer the matter to a trustworthy witness, the god at Delphi, and rely on the oracles which Chaerephon and a few others knew, those who cared about Socrates; but the things of which all the Greeks are witnesses, and which the Pythia uttered most commonly of all that ever were, and which all the future followed—these we shall nowhere set down to account, nor concede that they are the greatest testimonies to the wisdom of Themistocles? For where the same thing seemed good to that man and to the god concerning the safety of the whole, what else must one say? What, then, were the things ordained? It begins from somewhere on high, and then there is this which all babble of: "Wide-seeing Zeus grants to the Trito-born a wooden wall." Has the oracle, then, said this alone? No—but, as it were, it sets its seal upon the judgment by the addition. What, then, is this? "Alone to remain unsacked"—so that, lest, when these things were thus spoken, the Athenians should think the choice lay with them either to conquer by land or by sea, and lest they should grow soft, but should know that in the ships everything stands and that otherwise it is not possible to be saved. And further he magnified it in what follows, inasmuch as the god is leader of the Muses and best at speaking, surely. For he added: "It shall profit you and your children." What does he mean by this, "It shall profit you and your children"? Not on account of the children whom they conveyed to Troezen, it seems to me, but also those who would be hereafter. So were the triremes allotted together with the fortune of the city. For if ever they fared

well, it was in accordance with these that faring well belonged to them at all. And not even here did he stop his proclamation, but, as though forestalling and as though cutting short the censures of Plato, he presses on, sending forth every voice and saying outright already: "Do not you await the horsemen and the foot host coming in great numbers from the mainland in quiet, but withdraw." Then there is yet a final close: "You shall yet one day stand face to face with them." And I would gladly ask those who draw their deep beards, as one of the comic poets said, and exalt Plato up to this point: if in those times we had Plato, and affairs had been entrusted to him, and then the oracle came, what words would he think he ought to speak, or what would he have thought the Athenians ought to do? Or, by Zeus, if he himself did not happen to be general, what would he have advised Themistocles? These same things that the oracles advised, or the opposite of these? For if he was not going to know the meaning of the oracles, it was not the part of a wise man, what he was about to suffer; but if, knowing and understanding, he attempted to contradict, he was accomplishing the work of anyone rather than of Plato. For it would have been a demonstration of two extreme things, of impiety toward the god and of betrayal of the safety not only of the city but of all the Greeks. And if, however much, the god commanded one thing and Plato led another way, which ought Themistocles to have obeyed, or to which giving heed would he rightly have seemed to be of sound mind? For let them resolve this one of my perplexities and take their stand beside the tripod at Delphi, which the Greeks set up from the barbarians. But indeed it was not possible for a mortal to fight against a god. And indeed neither has it reason that, of those who die in Plato's city and polity, Plato himself entrusts the honors to the Pythia and lays it down as authoritative whatever seems good to her, but what the Pythia ordained for the safety of the living and the guarding of all Greece, this he should blame in the man who obeyed and

administered it. For by three of the greatest things the whole safety of the Greeks plainly came down almost to Themistocles alone: by his advising at the outset to build the triremes, before even any of the many expected the barbarians to come; by his persuading them, when the war was at hand, to fight at sea; and by his foreseeing in what part of the sea it would be advantageous. For if the triremes had not been built at the outset, there would have been no navy worth speaking of for the Greeks, nor one in which, taking courage, the rest would have combined; so that, while affairs on land were without resource and there was no power existing at sea, everything would have perished without a struggle; and if the ships existed, but it had seemed good to them to carry on the war in some other way, not even so would there have been any gain. And indeed the very nature of the sea made the multitude of ships useless to the barbarians. This was the terrible contest of Themistocles, and the preliminary contest among the Greeks, that he should remain and make them cease from looking toward the Isthmus. And some say there is even a fourth thing on behalf of Themistocles, that, besides the place, he also found out the time, joining the sea-battle when the wind was coming down; which indeed Phormion too later, as it seems, imitating, defeated the Lacedaemonians at sea off Naupactus. So far is Themistocles from having accustomed the Athenians to flee, or having corrupted their spirits. But I return to the rest of the oracle. So be it. What, then, did the god utter upon these things, and how did he set in order his counsel? "O divine Salamis, you will destroy the children of women." The god, then, called Salamis divine, as though there were going to be in it deeds greater than all human measure. But Plato says that the man who accomplished these things and brought them to Salamis ruined affairs and became no better than those who minister to pleasure. And Iacchus went forth and shared

in the rites, and clouds from the two goddesses descended upon the sea-battle, and gods and heroes, the common allies of the Greeks, fought together, and fought at sea with them, honoring Themistocles in deed; and the name was made exact for Salamis from every side and stood as divine for all. And yet, when Salamis heard this, it was surely the sea-battle that heard it; for Salamis was, in the time before, no other region's, but the god called the sea-battle divine through it. But Plato, as it seems, refuses the victory and condemns to death those who did these things, and prefers to perish august rather than to conquer with the gods. But Homer, had he survived, would have called the man who counseled and did these things "equal to Zeus in counsel," much more, it seems to me, than the general of the Cephallenians who smeared his ships with ruddle. For if Zeus gave the ships as a gift to Athena, and Apollo declared these things, and that man from the beginning was attuned to them and in the present alone knew the same things as the gods, how was he not destined to bear this address? But not so Plato; rather, in place of calling his judgment like and divine, like that of Zeus, he likens it to Sarambus and the tavern-keepers, all of them. How could anyone have used grandeur more out of season? Come, then, let us consider this too: if, as some of the heroes are already said to have been judged before divine judges, so Themistocles too, concerning what he advised, were tried before Pythian Apollo, which vote would the god have cast concerning him? The one that condemns? But it is absurd that he himself foretold these things and gave the oracle, but should condemn the one who obeyed. For where even Orestes is said to have been acquitted, when tried among the other gods, by referring the deed to Apollo, surely the man who pleads before Apollo himself, for things he accomplished with him,

there was no reason that he should be convicted. Then, the man whom it was not possible to convict before the god as judge—him did Plato think fit to accuse? And if he had been tried at Athens, with no such oracle existing beforehand, I mean, and then it had seemed good to those men to entrust the matter to the god, just as earlier, they say, the matter concerning the tribes—if the god had pronounced that he had deliberated nobly—he would thereafter have had to be acquitted, and it would have been permitted to no one to say anything else against this. But since the god forestalled the charge and acquitted him, and praised the deeds beforehand, before any man knew whether they would be done, and all but spoke in his support concerning everything from the beginning and brought forth in advance the judgment he held—nevertheless Plato has not held off, but has philosophized contrary to the oracle and has accused the deeds which, before they came to pass, one of the higher powers praised. Why, then, did you not also blame the Heraclids, my excellent friend, because they did not enter the Peloponnese by land, but crossed over from Rhium to Rhium? But I think that for them too it was the same as for the Greeks under Themistocles: by land they were to be overcome, but by sea it was possible both to be saved and to conquer. And here is a great sign: for as long as they tried the entry through the Isthmus, they fared ill, but when they came to the Achaean strait, they found it to be a strait of safety for them. Wherefore the god foretold to them to make the attempt through these narrows; but they, in ignorance, turning to the other way, almost perished utterly. And the same thing held also for those

. . . had then surrounded the Greeks. For some of them had perished at Thermopylae, while the others were everywhere victorious in their ships. There were straits, it seems, on both sides: against the one it was right to guard, the other one had to make use of. This too, I think, is why Themistocles judged that the Isthmus should be avoided above all else, guarding against it as though against some ancient curse, and put Salamis forward in its place. And indeed those men held the Peloponnese in no way more dishonourably or more obscurely than they held their post by the ships; rather, they proved to be the forefathers of many brave hoplites, men whom not even Plato anywhere ever reproached for their conduct in war, and they brought forth their descendants in greater honour than any other glory. For Plato himself sings the praises of that Dorian camp. This camp of Themistocles, then, was shown to have come about for the Greeks no less opportunely than that one. And that the Athenians became in no way worse than before in affairs on land, this the battle at Plataea showed, in which they had only the Lacedaemonians as rivals; the battle at Mycale showed it, in which they alone were given the first place of honour; and the battle later at Oenophyta showed it, by which they gained Boeotia and the Locrians and the Phocians. And if at some later time they did stumble, well, having once conquered at sea they did not always conquer there either; yet Themistocles was nowhere the cause of either of these reverses, since both forms of strength prevailed so greatly both during his life and for no short time after his death.

The deeds, then, and the policies of Themistocles down to the sea-battle and the flight of the King were of the kind that befit a man who, as I believe, more than any other human being escaped flattery, but came as far as any in intelligence and daring, joined with temperance and complete justice. As for his later affairs, what manner of things were they, to set them out

briefly? Mardonius was sending heralds to the Athenians on the King's behalf, having learned by deed that the balance of affairs lay with those men, and that whichever side they should join must of necessity prevail. The ambassador was Alexander, king of the Macedonians. But the Athenians, though they heard that he would rebuild their city for them and restore their land, though they heard of other acts of kindness besides, and of friendship and alliance for all time, were not lifted up by any of these offers, nor did they shame any part of what they had earlier accomplished; rather, they chose the danger undertaken on behalf of the Greeks instead of the gifts offered against the Greeks. The ambassador they let go—that he might not suffer the same fate as the earlier messengers—because of the dignity of his office as proxenos, but they ordered him to be gone at once, and in future to bring no such messages. Such was the harvest the Athenians reaped from the statesmanship and generalship of Themistocles. To such a pitch of courage and greatness of soul and of hatred for every ignoble servitude did he lead them all, that, when their city had been taken a second time, and Mardonius again sent his proposals—the council being then at Salamis and the herald having come from Athens—when someone in the council moved to accept them, they all gathered and stoned him to death, the men stoning him and the women stoning his wife: surely no more dishonourable a deed, Plato, nor one deserving of less praise, than the deeds of those women reared in your city, whom you bid take the field together with the men, doing this and that. Does Themistocles, then, seem to you to teach servility, or rather to be instructing in such things those who gathered about him? And so, when the Lacedaemonians came at about that same time to Alexander, and were appealing to him on behalf of the Greeks, and promising to maintain the Athenians' children and wives and those past the age of service so long as the war should last, so far was he from willing to accept even this, that he deemed them in need of pardon and sent them away, as men who did not know to whom they were sending an embassy. And of the same spirit too is the pillar

which, after these events, they set up, bearing this inscription: that Arthmius son of Pythonax, of Zeleia, both he himself and his family, be without rights and an enemy of the people of the Athenians, because he brought the gold of the Medes into the Peloponnese. For my part I do not know what decree Plato could have framed more nobly or more solemnly than this, on the same matter. And I observe this too, that both these resolves belong to the same philosophy: for the one forbade the Guardians to acquire gold, while the other had it recorded that the man who brought in the gold of the Medes was an enemy of the city, and that, if anyone should kill him, there should be no penalty. So then, the safeguard which Plato conceived for the best-governed city, that very safeguard Themistocles thought fit to provide for Greece; and this pillar the Athenians consecrated to the goddess, setting it beside the statue brought from Marathon, considering it in no way less honourable or less useful than their other dedications—a pillar on which is written how those who try to corrupt the Greeks ought to be treated. And it seems to me that both peoples are bound to cast every favourable vote on behalf of Themistocles. For all who consider safety the most fitting and the first of goods—it was Themistocles who secured it for all the Greeks; and all who judge affairs by greatness of spirit, and hold the dangers borne for noble ends, and a glorious name, more honourable than living in security, can find no finer examples than his. And so before both sets of judges he would justly win. And indeed, after the sea-battle, when all had gathered at the Isthmus and were bringing their vote from the altar of Poseidon concerning the prize of valour, here too there is something thoughtless one might charge against the

Greeks, but there is also the rest of their good sense to praise, and to take it as evidence for Themistocles. For each man, casting his vote first for himself, in the second place all alike cast it for Themistocles. The vote for first place, I think, belonged to that which by nature befalls all human beings—namely, that no one loves another more than himself; so that it had no force at all, but neither was it removed from pardon. The vote for second place, however, was already a clear token of the truth, and a sign that they could not have decided otherwise. So that, had it been declared from the outset that no one should cast his vote for himself but for another, all were going to cast it for Themistocles, whom indeed every one of them preferred above every other; and he would have become first in the same way as he then became second. So now too, by voting him into second place, they were doing the very same thing as if they had voted him into first. Yet not even so did he come away with the lesser share, but won in both. The first place he had received from the truth and from himself and held it; for he alone of all men did justly the very thing the others did. The second place had already been conceded to him; so that he was first out of them all. And when the Greeks had departed and were breaking up the assembly, since they saw what was happening—and here too they refuted themselves handsomely, showing that they were not acting honestly or as citizens should, and that they had not even passed those decrees on wholly just grounds, but rather, being throttled by the utmost necessity of their affairs, and not for any favour or goodwill—Themistocles so wholly despised them all that at the moment he gave it not the slightest thought, but, when affairs had settled, he came to Lacedaemon, as though on purpose. So poor a creature was he in his ways, and a very servant indeed. And the Lacedaemonians did not hold themselves in check at his coming; rather, while he was present they honoured him as they honoured none of their own kings, and when he departed,

they escorted him with three hundred chosen young men as far as the borders of Laconia—the only man, of Greeks or barbarians, of earlier times or of later, to be so honoured. So far did Themistocles seem to them to surpass all other human beings. And yet, when the best of the Greeks in affairs on land were not ashamed to escort that man to the borders of their own country, how is it open to us to blame him on account of the hoplites? Or how can we refuse to praise the man whom even those who seemed to be his rivals honoured, and against their will, with honours they gave to none of all who had ever lived?

There being three seasons, then, from which one might examine Themistocles, in each of them he will appear the best and the first of men. For before the barbarians came, he reconciled the cities, and remitted the charges held against the citizens exiled from the city; when the struggles came upon them, he did not fall out with the Lacedaemonians, and alone drove out the enemy; and when affairs had settled, and the Lacedaemonians wished to exclude from the treaty all the cities that had sided with the enemy, he spoke against it and prevented it, holding that something of the same kind would result as if Greece were declared an outcast from herself by her own act. For more than thirty cities would have had to fall into that calamity. So he did not think it fitting that Greece, having prospered so brilliantly and become so far superior to her enemies, should become so much less than she had been before. How could a man have been better, or more skilled in matters of state? And though I am able to speak also of his later misfortunes, and

how the whole business was contrived against him, and what manner of man he showed himself to be in these things too, I could have wished that my argument required me to press on and go through these matters as well; for I think I could say of him nothing inferior or less than what has already been said. But since this lies outside my subject, and length is creeping into the discourse, I shall pass these things over, adding only this much concerning this part also: that when it became necessary to march against Greece, he chose to die, by his deed dissolving every charge against him, and showing how highly he valued his former actions and policies, and that never, of his own free will, would he set anything before what was noble and fitting—not wealth, not children, not hopes, not safety itself. Then shall we slander him for the very things for which, that he might do nothing unworthy, he thought he ought to die? And shall we call a "servant" the man who never rendered any service to the Athenians against their will, nor ever thought it right to serve the King, but chose this end instead? And how would it not be shameful and monstrous, if, having no reverence for either his life or his death, we should so lightly defame him as this? For my part I think that the priests and priestesses and whoever else prays publicly at Athens might reasonably pray for this, each year, before all their other prayers—at least in those times and for as long as it was possible—that there be born among them a man like Themistocles, and that the land bring forth this good thing along with the rest of its produce. For they would seem to me to gain no less benefit than if all their crops had multiplied a hundredfold and yet more. In other circumstances I myself should have been ashamed to make use of witnesses so many and so great as those I have cited; but there is some advantage in one further testimony, which I must bring forward.
Let us consider, then, what manner of things Aeschines—the companion of Socrates and the

fellow-pupil of Plato—says to us about Themistocles. "Since, then, you have dared to lay hold of the life of Themistocles, consider what manner of man you have thought fit to censure. For reflect from where the sun rises and where it sets." "But there is nothing hard, Socrates," he said, "in knowing such things." "Has it then ever yet been a care to you that, of all that country as great as the sun traverses, which is called Asia, one man is ruler?" "Indeed yes," he said, "the Great King." "Do you know, then, that that man marched here and against the Lacedaemonians, thinking that, if he should subdue these two cities, he would easily have the rest of the Greeks subject to him? And he threw the Athenians into such fear that, abandoning their land, they fled to Salamis, having chosen Themistocles as general, and entrusted to him to deal with their affairs as he should wish. And indeed these were the greatest hopes of safety for the Athenians—whatever that man should resolve on their behalf. And it was not because the affairs of the Greeks were far inferior in the multitude of ships and infantry and money, while the King's prevailed, that Themistocles lost heart at the present circumstances; rather, he knew that, unless the deciding of counsel rested with him, the rest of their resources, great in size as they were, would be of no great help; and he had recognized this, that whichever side has men of greater seriousness in virtue set over their affairs, the affairs of those men too are wont to become superior. And so the King then perceived that his own affairs were weaker, on the day he met with a man more serious than himself. And Themistocles so easily handled the King's affairs, great as they were, that, after defeating him at sea, he wished to persuade the Athenians to break up the bridge of boats that the King had yoked together. But when he was unable to do so, he sent to the King the opposite of what had been resolved by the city—namely, that, though the Athenians were bidding him break the bridge, he himself was opposing it, trying to save the King and those with him; so that not only do we and the other Greeks consider Themistocles the cause of safety, but

the King himself, who had been defeated in war by him alone of men, believed he had been saved by that same man." So far did that man prevail by his intelligence. For this reason, when Themistocles was once made an exile from the city, the King repaid his gratitude as one who had been saved by him, and gave him many other gifts and granted him the governorship of all Magnesia, so that even in his exile his fortunes were greater than those of many Athenians reputed to be men of nobility and worth who stayed at home. Who, then, in that time, could justly be charged with being the most powerful, other than Themistocles, who, taking command of the Greeks, overthrew the man who reigned from the rising of the sun to its setting? "Consider then, Alcibiades," I said, "that for that man, being such as he was, knowledge so great as his did not prove sufficient to guard him against being driven out and made dishonoured by the city; rather, it fell short. What then do you suppose holds for base men, who are at no pains over themselves? Is it any wonder if they cannot manage rightly even small things? And do not condemn me, Alcibiades," I said, "as one disposed strangely and impiously toward fortunes and divine things, if I credit that man with knowledge of all that he did, and think that no fortune was the cause of these works. For I could far more readily prove to you that those who hold the contrary opinion to mine are impiously disposed than that they could prove it of me—men who think that fortunes come equally to the wicked and to the good, rather than that, for those who are noble and good, being also more pious, the things that come from the gods are better." It is, then, the same Socrates who speaks both here and there; yet in Plato's discourses he appears to name Themistocles a servant and a menial, and to set him among the flatterers, while in the passages we have just now produced he bids us count him the best of the Greeks, and credits him with knowledge of all his affairs, and thinks fit to make no fortune the cause, but holds that everything belonged to that man's judgement. As for me, this addition I do not

accept, but I think the good fortune should be held the cause of all noble things; that these statements, however, do not agree with those, I prove. For if all this is merely an argument spoken on both sides, and one must carry through the rest of it in accordance with whatever thesis one has taken up, then let this be granted, and we seek nothing further: in any case, even so, our part is blameless. But if it is spoken in earnest, with just seriousness, and contains a judgement of the truth, which of the two must we trust, when these statements appear contrary to those? And indeed I should never set Aeschines on an equal footing with Plato—may I never so contend!—but let that judgement be left to the absurd among the sophists; I say rather that the greater and more perfect Plato is in discourse, the more, at least in the matter of Themistocles, one ought to accept that other account. For Aeschines, it is likely, says what he heard, or what comes closest to it; whereas Plato, I think, makes use of the abundance of his nature, just as he sets out countless other things in the name of Socrates, things which it is agreed that Socrates never concerned himself with—doing, I think, what is just in this very thing too, and the work of a most excellent man, namely to think it right to adorn one's teacher; except that to this it befits him to add also the unwillingness to disgrace others who do not deserve it.

These, then, are the things which it was reasonable to say about these men, leaving out none of the necessary points, yet not thinking it right to say everything in order, lest we should seem to anyone to lack taste. He insists, however, on the points where they stumbled in their dealings with the public, as if, because some thought worse of them, it were fitting for us to consider them worse, or, because certain others wronged them, it were necessary for us too not to refrain from heaping insults on them. But I should not have thought it right for anyone else to reproach them with these things, far less Plato; but rather

to remember the saying: "And how am I the worse, if so-and-so strikes me unjustly on the cheek?" For whether a man is exiled, or punished with money or with death, or suffers any other such thing, fortune is surely the mistress of it; but their discourses and their statesmanship, derived from what they deliberately chose, it is just to examine—and in these I do not see how I could ever pardon myself, were I to think it right to accuse them. "For it is not reasonable," he says, "for those educated by them to wrong them, nor, from those things by which they became better, to vote anything unjust." But I, for my part, would not say that they erred in that by which they became better, but rather in that they were unable to become wholly like them. And of this I find there is much excuse on both sides. For neither that men should not err at all—and these a popular assembly—nor that one should be able to make all men sinless, would anyone advance as a serious charge. For where it is not easy, and perhaps not even possible, for a single man in private life once and for all to escape blame, surely one ought to think the same of so great a city. But indeed, where even for those who erred there is reasonably pardon, surely for those who lead them toward what is best, and whom they would not obey when they erred, it would be monstrous if we should not grant it. Plato, then, does not allow us to consider the matters in which, by following them, they succeeded; but the wrongs they did against those very men—so far were they from doing what those men thought right—these he charges against them. And the benefits they reaped from their education he passes over; but the things that were not part of what they were taught, but rather remnants of human nature, these he lays upon those men who did everything in their power that they might do no wrong—just as if someone should declare that the schoolmasters who showed the boys their letters and taught them to write, so far as was possible, were the cause of the errors in these matters, if afterwards they should write something not finely nor as they

ought, of their own accord. But these things are not among what the teacher showed them beforehand, nor among what they were taught; rather, he set forth how they should write rightly, and what they do preserve, they preserve of his teachings, while these are their own errors—whether through want of learning, or through carelessness, or however else they came to follow—save that they are not at all on his account, nor on account of what came from him, no more than those who lack sustenance lack it on account of those who provided and gave it to them. But all these things, I think, are matters of deficiency, not of what one shared in, nor of what one reaped so far as was possible. If, then, those men taught the Athenians anything worse, let that be said against them, and no argument will excuse them from being base; but if they did not educate all, nor as exactly as possible, nor as much as they wished, why should one set down to their leadership what escaped it? For it was not from their company that the people got this; rather, in this very respect they got nothing from those men. So it was not from what they attended to in them that they erred, but from what they did not attend to that they went wrong. Thus, in the matters in which they obeyed, those who persuaded them clearly persuaded them well. Then again, music and geometry and the other arts—I mean even the quite humble ones—not all who attend their teachers acquire, but out of the many a very few; and not even in these does anyone compel the teachers themselves to be held responsible for unfailing exactness throughout, nor, if the learner does not succeed in everything, nor become like the one who taught him, does anyone set this down against that teacher as beyond dispute—neither as though he knew nothing of the art, nor as though he willfully held back, nor, to put it altogether, as doing wrong. But we know the saying of Homer, which he spoke about sons and which holds good in such cases too: "Few sons," he says, "are like their father;
the more are worse, and few are better than their father." And it has fallen out that one becomes like his teacher and another not, and the one becomes worse, the other better. So

we know it to be in families and in arts. But if Themistocles and Pericles and Miltiades and Cimon did not educate all the Athenians in statecraft, nor make them all in succession better, tribe by tribe and man by man, distributing knowledge like a festival-dole, shall we then say we have discovered something monstrous against them—that they themselves were no better than anyone else at these things? And you do not accuse the potter because he did not teach all men in succession to mould clay; yet you accuse the foremost among the Greeks because they did not make all men like themselves? And you are not content with the saying of your Protagoras—that if they advanced the many even in the slightest toward the better—but rather, if the people did not handle everything blamelessly and as a single man would, this you now turn against their leaders.

And indeed I observe that even the physicians, and those reputed to be very excellent, do not so utterly remove diseases that not even a trace remains in the body, but often leave some of the old ailments behind and reckon the relief they give sufficient cause for gratitude, and are not able by their complete treatments to overcome nature itself, but free a man from this disease while in no way hindering another from coming on later. For the art is not adequate to the very end, but nature prevails. What wonder, then, if those men too, having given the Athenians much good counsel and prevented many of their troubles, were not able to hold them to the end nor to heal them immortally, but were overcome by the nature of the populace—or, if one must say it, of mankind in common—and were not able once and for all to root injustice out of the city, like farmers cutting away each year the things that ravage the land, yet not reaching through the whole of the seed? If in this way some seed of injustice and folly, inevitably, escaped them too when they wished to purge the city, and remained, and not everything obeyed them, but there were things the people deliberated on their own account, what baseness does this entail for these men? Or why should one reckon the deeds of others against them—just as if, there being civil strife in the city, and these men leading the

one party, that of the decent men, someone should then attribute to those very men the errors of the others and of those who wronged them? And what nature has it, that men who neither did these things, but moreover thought fit to prevent them, should be blamed? But perhaps it is not right to bring the charge against them, yet right to bring it on their behalf. And indeed, for my part, I have reflected how profitably to Plato himself I clear away these charges, and what manner of handles he himself gives against himself out of these accusations, if anyone should wish to imitate him. For consider, by the gods: if, as they say of Protesilaus that he obtained leave to come among the living again from those below, or as one of the comic poets represented four of the leaders rising from the dead—among whom two of these are included—if in this way these four men of ours, concerning whom the present trial is, should obtain a resurrection, so as to be with Plato for one single day to discuss these matters; and then they were to speak, putting forward Pericles, or, if you like, Themistocles, who would stand for us upon the wing of the orators—and let no one reckon against me the harshness of the reply; for in the main there will be nothing of the sort, but we shall remit it so far as we can, and then one must suppose the words to be theirs and not mine. "He that scrapes, let him scrape back" even at the asses, the proverb surely grants; but Pericles the sons of Homer would liken rather to the lions than to the asses. So this much freedom of speech it will be permitted to grant him: as much as, if no one thinks it right to give judgement against Plato, would also let that man not be debarred from teaching from these same matters. And if anyone shall be vexed at these things on Plato's behalf, he will do the very opposite of what he wishes. For by the same things by which he will declare that Plato is being slandered, by these he will confirm how Plato slanders. But indeed, if he shall think it well, even for those reviled, to use the same handles, and

these not to revile in return, but to clear their own case through that man's words, how will he bid us count it clever in Plato that he spoke ill first of things which no one compelled him to, and by which he supposed he was showing those men to be worse?

They will then say, as I believe, this—or rather, let me speak as in their own person: "We, Plato, though we have heard from you many slanderous things, will not requite you with the like, nor speak ill of you, but consider you a man among the foremost and the best of the Greeks, and we rejoice with the city, not with you alone, at your nature. Altogether, from the beginning we have made it our own windfall, whatever our city should gain. And the finest of all gains is the bearing of good men—among whom we too once thought we belonged, though you do not grant it. And since you liken us also to Mithaecus, who wrote up the Sicilian cookery, it is likely that you know these things better than we do. For we know nothing of such writings, since we did not frequently mix in Sicily. But just as you had no leisure for affairs of state because of your discourses in philosophy, so we, because of our discourses in statecraft, had no leisure to learn anything of those matters there. But it is not unlikely that you should fall in with such men and writings, even if not willingly but unwillingly—just as, no doubt, you got experience of many other things even willingly, having often been conveyed across the Sicilian sea. Come then, by the very table in Sicily—whether Mithaecus set it forth or anyone else whatever—what proof have you of our baseness? That, by Zeus, we did not make all the Athenians just. But did you make Dionysius any better—if you like, the son of Hermocrates, or, if you like, the son

of Dionysius? For you consorted with both of them. And what benefit did they reap from you and your company? And yet you surely discoursed with them about justice and law and the constitution, and you praised to them also the equality found in geometry, and they were so fond of listening that they even sent for you, and you fell short in nothing of eagerness, that their cities might fare well through them. But you failed to notice that you yourself were caught in all the proverbs—carding wool into the fire, and boiling a stone, and sowing the rocks. For what did those men reap of your admonitions and discourses? What of divine or human matters did they manage better after that day on which they lent you their ears? What repentance for their former errors came upon them? What love of philosophizing, leaping over all else? What did they get better than the men within the city itself, or those outside it? Which of the people of Gela or Leontini, or the other Greeks in Sicily, obtained those good and just men through you and your discourses? And if none of the Greeks, to which of the barbarians—to whom of those in Sicily—did they show that they had become better? Very well. But of those dwelling in Sicily to none; yet of the barbarians or Greeks in Italy, to whom, tell me, did they conduct themselves more nobly than before? Toward what and toward what men did your statesmanship make them better? To which of the Carthaginians—if you cannot name the Greeks—or to which of the other barbarians in Libya did the tyrant display himself practising virtue, from the time he listened to Plato's teachings, whether I mean the elder or the younger? And indeed, if one must lay upon the counsellors the errors of those in power, why will men say you accuse us rather than yourself? Since it is possible to allege against you also the deeds of those men. But if you should say that these are nothing to you, by these same arguments you also acquit us, if the people of the Athenians did anything outside what we thought best. I think, then, that this will not suffice these men, but that they would now most gladly add a further point. Of what kind? This: 'Since, then, in both cases it is possible that not everything was done as the counsellor

thought best, which of us set about the task with the better and juster business—the man who thought fit to educate the tyrant and sailed so far from his fatherland, or those who were willing to give their own citizens the best counsel, and to make their affairs better from what was possible? What do you say, Plato, to this?' they will ask; 'and since, once and for all, we did not prevail, which of us came nearer to our original purpose? And which of us advanced things further? Did we make the Athenians better, or you the tyrants? And indeed, for them, except perhaps in a few things, everything has gone wrong, whereas for those who acted with us everything, except for a few things, has been done more nobly than among all mankind. By so much did we show those who dealt with us to be better than you showed those who dealt with you. And if you shall say that these were better by nature, by this too you prove us the wiser, if we placed some hopes in such men, and did not, as you did, wholly fail of the mark, having thought it of some use to converse with those tyrants. Then, just as you allege their nature in the things in which they became better than others, so, if they seem to you to have acted somewhat too rashly, set this down to that same nature, and do not bring it against us; nor, while the things they accomplished under our leadership you take away from the counsellors and from us who helped bring them to pass by being thought to have advised the best, do you say that the wrongs they committed against us, on their own account, are wrongs that we do. For of the former we too are in part the cause, but of the latter not even a little. But these things, as Sophocles said, are matters of suffering rather than of doing. And indeed, if to give offence and to meet with some calamity is proof of baseness and carries a just reproach for the one who suffers, consider our case and your own. What benefit did you reap from the tyrants whom you chose to educate? Did not Polycrates—" the

fortune that came from without—"was no better than ours to you either. Thus from the beginning, contrary to all hope and contrary to all your worth, you were shut up and reared; and if a certain Italian Greek of the Pythagoreans had not begged you off—just as you say of the chief magistrate, that he prevented one of us who was about to be cast into the pit—you yourself perhaps would have fallen into the stone-quarries, or at any rate, the second time, you would not have escaped 'the sheer streams of the Styx-water' of the strait, but would have died there in Sicily. As it is, it was Archytas who prevented it, and Dionysius was ashamed before Archytas when he sent his message and granted the favour, but he was not ashamed before Plato, with whom he had consorted and from whom he had heard those fine and solemn discourses; rather, so far was he from honouring or obeying him as he spoke, that, in order not to hear your voice, he kept you shut up like some 'worthless vagabond.' And the lot of Cimon befell you—that lot which you say the Athenians inflicted on him, unwilling to hear his voice—nor did Dionysius then think you worthy even of that, save that you were not on equal terms. For Cimon the Athenians removed so that they might not hear him for ten years, but for you it was not even possible to remove yourself, though surely you wished it and sought it, having sense, as I declare. But this was the dreadful calamity: that it was not possible to depart, but you had to remain by force and all but be nailed fast. And then your dearest friend hands you over, after these things, to a Spartan, Pollis, and not even there did he stay his outrage, but ordered that you be sold—sold, alas, the best of the Greeks, like a slave bound for export. He, that man hated by the gods, would not have committed this outrage had we been living and our triremes in being. Yet he ordered it, and Plato was led out of Sicily by Pollis, and Pollis in his turn, taking charge of you, was ashamed even before the absent Dionysius and remembered what he had enjoined, but seeing you and being in your company set you at nothing; rather, your marvellous power and persuasiveness in discourse was overcome by the commands of Dionysius. And Pollis sided with that man, and that too when he had given such

orders, but with you not at all. Let us add that, though a Spartan and one reared in the laws and constitution which holds second place of all in your own judgement—or rather, first of those that exist. And in vain, it seems, were all those many praises sung by you of the city of the Lacedaemonians. At any rate, the man who was once the admiral of the Lacedaemonians fell as far short of your worth as not even any one of the Persians or Scythians could have done, who had no power to understand your voice at all. And yet, if you thought fit that he should become better than Dionysius concerning you, and should resolve on something better, but he paid you no heed, but belonged to the absent man and to the one who had enjoined the basest things—how are you not utterly inferior to the tyrant? And in what respect are you justified in bringing it forward, if anyone undertaking to persuade another failed? But if you thought fit to be content with the present circumstances, while he had no respect for your silence, nor held it more sufficient than all words to set before himself the fitting reckonings concerning you—how did you obtain what was likely, or how did you reap what befitted the nature of your own self? 'By Zeus, but you are in no way worse, if Pollis and Dionysius were beside their senses.' Nor are we either, blessed sir, if some Athenian proved base toward us. So then, to such a pitch of excess did Pollis come, and was so very earnest, on being made master to deliberate concerning a man such as he had not hoped for even in a dream, and then to be shown to have deliberated something most magnificent and surpassing in humanity and culture, that, conveying you to Aegina—in which death had been proclaimed for any Athenian caught setting foot there—there he disembarks you. And here again you met with the lot of Themistocles, or rather you fared even better. For he came to the Molossians, to Admetus, an enemy

of his, and through him was saved; and to you it happened to be brought to trial among the common enemies of your own fatherland. And if those men had not proved better than the tyrant and his servant—and these too, doing well, were ashamed before the philosophy and reputation of Plato—you would have died there on the spot, having exchanged island for island, in the very forecourt of your fatherland, not in Sicily: so much were you going to gain. But the worthy fellow-voyager, the Spartan, did not even thus forget what he had heard from Dionysius, but sold your sacred head; and while Pollis was selling you, no one of the Greeks would buy you—so wholly were all of them gripped by your discourses—but a Libyan, a man named Anniceris, whom not one of mankind would even have known, had he not made use of your misfortunes. As it was, he did not buy Plato, but reputation for himself and the being known. And then at last Dion played the part of the marvellous benefactor, sending the ransom to the Libyan. But not even that man was outdone by Dion; rather, he released you free of charge—a man who had never before set eyes on you nor consorted with you anywhere, on islands or mainland. Coming home, then, and having escaped, like some Odysseus, not deaths only but slavery as well, and having so plainly owed your deliverance to the baseness and the kindness of others, you kept quiet for a time; but when, the elder Dionysius having died, the Dionysius who sprang from him took over the rule and summoned you again to the much-hymned Sicily—as though, along with the other things he had inherited from his father, he had inherited also the outrage against you, and were heir also of giving you orders, as to the Syracusans or the others in Sicily—you went sailing off. And of what

kind of treatment you reaped in turn, you yourself know: how you accomplished none of the things for which you set out, and endured many things of every sort, and these on behalf of anything rather than yourself; having only this one piece of good fortune—for it shall be said—that you did not share the lot of Philoxenus the dithyrambic poet, although in your conduct you were, in a way, his very counterpart. Do not suppose that we are ignorant of your discourses, or do not agree that they are true—that it is not lawful for a better man to be outraged or harmed by a worse. We know these things and bear witness that you speak truly; yet nonetheless that marvellous lover of yours left out not one bit of outrage and wantonness. And you perhaps were in no way outraged, but he, by the things he thought were outrages, did more of them than by those through which he knew he would do you honour. And not even so did you put an end to your association with that man and to your voyaging; but having, contrary to hope and contrary to your worth, been so released and gladly brought safely home again, you were so far from being able to give counsel to others that you did not even counsel yourself, which was all that remained. But the proverb, and Homer too, says: 'The fool knows a thing once it is done.' Yet you, the wisest of the Greeks, were not even thus instructed; rather, Dionysius mastered you again, holding out kindly hopes, and again in turn you made trial of the evils of tyranny, sailing a third time, just as wrestlers wrestle—twice having stumbled against the same man, and the third time stumbling altogether against a tyrant and a tyrannical household.

So neither did you yourself run all your course before a fair wind. Why then do you cast fortune in our teeth, when you yourself have had such experience of it? It is as if Odysseus should reproach Menelaus with his wandering: 'My good man, I too came home not with all my company, but with more

of them than you, and sooner than you, and having sailed an unequal course; and moreover without meddling, as you did, sitting in Sicily beside the Cyclops.' But, O Plato, most marvellous of all men, do not thrust with both hands—and that not through one of your friends and one of your enemies, but through yourself and these men, whom it were more reasonable to consider friends; or, if not, look not for what you will charge but for what you will first answer in your own defence: so many are your own affairs too. And yet you think fit to mock even the dithyrambic poets, as men set in motion only toward pleasure and gratification. But it appears that Dionysius, when he could not bring Philoxenus the Cytherian once more under his power, but that man wrote to him freely 'Go and weep,' yet got you a second and a third time into his grip after those first sojourns. You will say the pretext is a fine one for you: that you did and said all these things for the sake of Dion's affairs. Nobly indeed do you both say it and do it. Consider then our pretext too, and if you find it more dishonourable, or that we meddled for the sake of small ends, take and brand us, and become a Dionysius instead of a Plato toward us. But if, just as you endured all these things for Dion's sake and for his hospitality and friendship, so we, on behalf of the common hearth of our fatherland and of the common treaties and rights—some of us of the city, some even of the Greeks—undertook to say and do and suffer anything whatever, reverencing all the titles of Zeus, reverencing the titles and honours of all the other gods, and besides

the heroes and our common ancestors, and the memory of the time past and the reckoning of the age to come, and all the things that are held greatest among all men, both Greeks and barbarians—if then anything turned out contrary to our intention from these endeavours, why do you accuse us of what is not yours? And indeed, if this too must be added: we, if we did stumble somewhat, yet stumbled having acted on behalf of the things we were earnest about, whereas you did so straightaway from the very beginning. So then, if to have met with some troubles is a reproach and a censure for the counsellor, you have met with no fewer than we. And there is added the fact that you accomplished none of the things you wished. But if the deliberate choice itself must be examined by itself, then your part is reasonably blameless—and from the same considerations our part is blameless too. And there is added the fact that we mastered our affairs, and that these are greater than both the things you were earnest about and the things in which we ourselves stumbled. You, then, thinking to refute us, speak against yourself; while we, speaking on our own behalf, also tend to your case. Or rather, in your defence we too have a share, but you have not as much as we. So that, if anyone shall spare us, it is unclear whether he will spare you too; but if anyone shall condemn you, he might perhaps pardon us; and if again he will not even spare us, hardly will he spare you. Thus our winning comes about on your behalf. In view of this, look not to mine, but to yours too,' as Teucer said to someone, and do not wish to examine everything exactly, nor, there being three things to which one might look—judgement, deeds, fortune—dismissing the two, lay hold of the third, and that too when the greatest part even of this is on our side. For if we had had to foreknow these things from the start and yet deliberately give ourselves up on behalf of Greece, we should not have shrunk back, nor fallen so far short of Codrus,

and you too, I think, would have given this very counsel.' Since—come, by friendship—which would you rather have wished: that neither the things accomplished through us had been done for the city, nor that any of the citizens had wronged us—well then, others were going to wrong both us and them—or that, for the sake of those deeds, they should be done, even if it had to turn out so? I, for my part, think the latter. So then, since you would say you would rather have both than neither, you agree both that to us, who took part in public affairs, belongs everything that befits, and that more largely we are the cause of what tends to the city's good repute. How then were you not more justly bound to praise than to blame? For if, even to those very men who wronged us, what was well deliberated and done is of more account, and one might not unreasonably remit these things to them, how is it not just that we be released from all blame—we who have no part whatever in the accusations, but of the things that come under praise, if you are willing to speak the truth, have the greatest share? We then, though we could exalt ourselves in many ways, pass it by. But that you may know how much fairness is ours, and how far in every way we are from wishing to grasp more than our due, let the whole be common; take away, if you will, all the additions above; let us settle on equal terms—we are surely not inexperienced in treaties—and let neither you make mention to us of misfortunes, nor we use this against you. For there is no middle ground: either we too must be convicted along with you by these arguments, or both you and we must be let off guiltless, and it must suffice that certain others wronged us." When they had said these things, I think, they would readily go back again to join the majority—if indeed those men too must be thought to lie among the majority, as I, for one, do not think. I, then, should most gladly acquit them both; but if anyone thinks otherwise, the poets would call him "hard of heart." Come, then, let us also examine his examples.

"Good charioteers, then," he says, "do not at first fall out of their cars; but once they have tended their horses and themselves become better charioteers, then they fall out." And somewhere higher up, among the things directed against Pericles, he says: "A keeper of asses and horses and oxen, being of such a kind, would be thought bad, if, having taken them over not kicking nor butting nor biting, he showed them doing these things from wildness." But, my good man, you speak of the same individual asses and horses and oxen; whereas, of the same Athenians, all of these, I think, were leaders—Solon, I mean, and Cleisthenes and Miltiades and Pericles, and whoever each was. But the city is one, and the name one, while the men are different and different through the ages. What wonder, then, that some met with gentler and more tractable subjects, and others with rougher and more spirited—just as countless other things, surely, change with the times? For we do not gather even the fruits of the earth alike year by year—I mean neither in quantity nor in quality. Rather, the strength of the year is held to be no less than that of the land. So that, if in the earlier time the Athenians, being of easier natures, in the days of those men were already hard to hold in check, the affliction would not be outside the whole of nature—just as, with time advancing, I think, their spirit too would change according to their misfortunes. Furthermore, charioteers do not corrupt horses by this—that they train some and fail with others—but rather if they make worse the very ones they had before as good and faultless; whereas Miltiades and those after him did not have the same subjects throughout, but some were added, surely, and some passed away, and some even quit their company. How then is it just that they be judged against the charioteers, or how, as though the same horses remained theirs, must they so render account? It is as if someone should think fit that the Molionidae, and the horses of Diomedes the Thracian, should be

ruled in the same way as those one had from the start. And indeed the charioteers each rule their own cars by themselves, and no one interferes; and I say this very same thing concerning the keepers of the asses and the oxen; so that, if anything were mishandled, they would reasonably bear the blame securely. But not Pericles, nor Themistocles; nor did any of those men rule the Athenians alone, nor freed from anyone undertaking to do the opposite; rather, many others, surely, managed affairs of state along with them, having neither the same natures nor the same judgements; so that one ought to assign the errors to these still more than to those. For I, for my part, would say they belonged to those men by so much the more, as the wrongs were done against them. But, to speak simply, how is it just to demand a reckoning from those alone who were not the sole causes of affairs? We do not, then, blame the original charioteers, if another, taking over the same horses, shows them to be worse; rather, both charioteers and teachers win greater repute when others, set in charge of the same subjects, prove unequal to them. And, by Zeus, if even at the same time—say, on the same day—another, taking over the chariot, mounts it, the good charioteer, the famous one, is no longer answerable for the whole; but if once and for all the care is settled upon him, then these matters too are so judged, and no one inherits the misdeeds of another. But this very thing too is a base accusation—that they did not allow the better man and the one not of their own party to use his art, but tripped him up, like those in the foot-races. So too, then, concerning the statesmanship of those men: until you show that, while the philosophers reigned and were alone set over affairs, these errors were committed—I mean of Miltiades, of Themistocles, of Pericles, of

Cimon—do not by any means lay the blame on philosophy herself. But if you are able to refute these men by themselves, use this method and show their errors; if not, you accuse the asses rather than their keepers. For if there were no errors before those men engaged in statecraft at Athens, but all these things began from Miltiades and Themistocles and from those men, it would be another argument; nor, if some others took part in statecraft at the same time as those, would I mention it, but I grant that those men alone are accountable for everything. But if it is likely that something else too had been erred before, why do we blame the Laconians for these things? For surely you, at any rate, are permitted to jest, since this very thing—that the calamities are ancient, and, as you somewhere say, beginning from Theseus, and perhaps even from yet earlier, and that these men were not the first to stumble—I shall let pass. And yet Theseus, though exiled and destroyed, dying in Scyros, did not remain dishonoured in the eyes of the god, but the god commanded the Athenians to bring back his bones, many ages later, as they say. But nonetheless I shall let these things pass. Yet your argument about these men has gone to ruin on you. For by the fact that you have accused all of them with the same charges, you have undone what you think you hold as strong. Why? Because this charge might perhaps belong to Miltiades, but no longer to Themistocles; and if to both Miltiades and Themistocles, yet not to Cimon; and if to Miltiades and Themistocles and Cimon, yet surely not also to Pericles, but to him least of all. For Themistocles took them over from Miltiades already butting, and Cimon from Miltiades and Themistocles, and Pericles from Miltiades and Themistocles and
Cimon. Thus Pericles least of all was accountable, the very man whom you accused most of all, and likened, apart from the rest, to the bad keepers of asses and oxen.

Let us reflect, then, also on what we were just now speaking of: the association of Plato himself with Dionysius. For if this is the one true and just and sufficient defence and excuse on Plato's behalf, of all defences, concerning the offences the tyrant committed both while Plato was with him and again after he had withdrawn—namely, that even before he saw Plato and heard his discourses he had done many things of every kind—what prevents us, on behalf of those men too, from saying not that the affairs of the people are on equal footing with those of the tyrants, but rather that the wrongs done before their statesmanship were less than those committed by the tyrants from the start, and that the wrongs done during their statesmanship deserve not equal censure with those of the tyrants from the time they admitted Plato; and what prevents us from saying this very thing in common—that even before those men set about speaking, there were errors at Athens, and if these were less than those of Dionysius, then surely the later ones too were not comparable to his, but were such as men, being human, are likely to err? Come then, let us also consider and go through the things that befell these men. For the people did not so condemn all of them, nor did they suffer these things by a common decree, nor, to begin with, did all suffer the same. How could they? Rather, Themistocles and Cimon were ostracized.
